It melds rigorous economic reasoning with a clear goal of environmental stewardship, using techniques such as cost-benefit analysis, market-based incentives and game theory to tackle real-world issues. Be it evaluating the success of cap and trade schemes or placing an accurate economic value on resource extraction, environmental economics offers practical strategies toward sustainability.

I am also enthusiastic about the highly interdisciplinary nature of environmental economics. # Tips for Starting and Keeping a Neighborhood Book Club Alive

Getting started: Identify neighbors who might be interested, perhaps with a posting, an email, or a casual conversation. 6 to 12 members is a good size that encourages a lot of discussion without being unwieldy. Decide on a regular, consistent meeting time (whether it's weekly, biweekly or monthly) and location- someone’s home, a coffee shop, library, etc.

Selecting books: Allow members to choose the next book with members submitting suggestions and voting for the next book to read. Variety is good. Novels with between 200-300 pages often are preferred and do not require too long to read before a meeting (normally 4-6 weeks).

Running the meeting: Share snacks or light fare to start. Aim for 60-90 minutes for discussion. Begin with members' general thoughts and then follow the discussion guide (or go with where the conversation takes you) covering characters, plots, writing style, etc. 

Make sure to let quieter members participate, too. 

Have a book discussion leader for each meeting, ideally rotating responsibility among members.

Keeping momentum: Having everyone take turns hosting and supplying snacks alleviates workload. Mix up what members read, moving from popular, modern works to classics and more obscure works. Invite guest speakers (local authors or librarians). Address a lack of attendance promptly by reiterating expectation or checking in with the absent member.

Maintaining interest: Occasionally plan themed potlucks, attend author events as a group, and call authors for a group conversation on video. Build an online sharing list (Goodreads is a good option), and plan activities to celebrate milestones (your book club’s anniversary, for instance). Most people belong to book clubs for the social interaction, as much as reading.

Troubleshooting: If there are discussions or differing views over book choices, remind members that discussion, reading of different perspectives, makes for stronger discussions. If the book club seems to be going flat, survey members on what they’d like to read in the future. Starting a book club is low-effort, high-reward, in building both community and neighborhood connection, as well as stimulating personal intellectual growth.

# Top 10 Easy Scopes for Newbies

Want to star hop without draining your bank account? I totally get it. Here are my 10 secrets to choosing your very first telescope without a full-blown identity crisis or the fear of missing rent.

1.  Your Bank Account is King (Really!). A pricey $5,000 scope isn't necessary for an awe-inspiring cosmic trip. The sweet spot for an excellent beginner scope is between $100–$300, give or take.

2.  Keep It Simple: Refractors or Dobsonian. Compared to complicated mounts, these beauties are extremely user-friendly. They require no real learning curve, making them absolutely perfect for newcomers.

3.  Power Isn't Everything-In Fact, It's Pretty Overrated. High magnification might sound impressive on paper, but a 6-inch reflector will knock your socks off without any fancy, pricey eyepiece investments.

4.  Bigger Lenses for Better Views. Aperture is the single most crucial factor when choosing a scope. If your finances allow for it, aim for at least a 4-inch lens.

5.  Shake is for Rockstars, Not Telescopes. An inexpensive, wobbly mount can turn a celestial viewing session into a maddening experience. Prioritize a sturdy, solid mount for your mental well-being!

6.  Don't Skip the Reviews. I strongly recommend checking out astronomy forums and YouTube for in-depth scope reviews. Real users will never be afraid to call a terrible scope out for what it is.

7.  Eye-popping Eyepieces. A good quality set of eyepieces can make a world of difference to your observing experience, so don't automatically go with a junk set that often comes packed with scopes.

8.  Portability Factor. Does your celestial vision require you to hike it outside? If so, be realistic about what you're able to move around.

9.  Ease of Setup. You want a scope you can set up, grab, and go without a lengthy, time-consuming setup that requires you to assemble a dozen different pieces.

10. Join the Club! Astronomy clubs have experienced members who will be more than happy to let you get hands-on with different scopes and give brutally honest advice-you might even get a chance to borrow gear.

The most important thing about choosing a telescope is actually using the darn thing. So make sure you find one that excites you and complements your way of life. I hope you enjoy your journeys across the night sky!

# AI Generated Children's Book Illustration and ethics

The use of AI generated illustrations in children's books presents many interesting ethical considerations. One argument in favor of AI generated illustrations in children's books hinges on the increase in the book's affordability. AI technologies will lower the cost for creating an illustrated children's book that an independent, and potentially small, publisher or authors can produce within a reasonable price range. 

These technologies, in this case,, will Democratize Illustration for the independent writer of children's books who can't necessarily afford to outsource for an illustrator. 

However, there is the issue of fair artists rights. Not only are AI programs trained on existing images that could very well belong to a professional illustrator and were generated without explicit permission for AI generation training in some or potentially most, but also by lowering prices for illustrated children's books, professional, potentially poor, writers might lose out on yet another opportunity. Beyond artist rights is also the fact that children's illustration carries an inherent value in teaching children about how to view representations of themselves, beauty and how they view different forms of diversity. AI illustrations often produce homogenized images that may not represent children and the diversity of their world. 

Ultimately children books still carries a pedagogical meaning to children. 

AI-generated pictures that are produced simply on account of expediency disregard the meaning they carry in building relation between author and reader in a world which encourages this, but devalues the part that humans carry to this relationship. The best option for future use of AI-generated work in children's illustrations might be to have a "marked" system where children and parents know when illustrations are created via AI, or to allow use while demanding fair compensation for artist data used for training programs, or by working alongside human artists and only supplementing human artists rather thanreplacing them. There must be some careful thought as AI and illustrative art in children's literature continues to advance or children could suffer and the value of illustrated books, a truly meaningful medium, diminishes.

# The Right to Repair Movement is Becoming a Reality With More People Refurbishing their Electronics

For years, the world has been accumulating more and more electronics waste, and there are now several movements that seek to allow consumers to repair and reuse their electronic devices rather than throwing them away, breaking thethrowaway culturethat many have come to associate with the technology industry.

Therepair-and-refurbish,movementseeks to give consumers the ability to repair their laptops, computers, and phones without having to pay top dollar for a repair from the original manufacturer. It argues that repairing our devices will decrease the amount of electronics waste we produce, save us money, and can extend the life of an appliance or cell phone that would normally still be in perfect working condition with only a small defect.

“Consumers shouldn’t have to go out and buy a new laptop just because the screen breaks or the laptop is outdated or the battery dies on my laptop,”said a repair advocate. Now that independent repair services are blooming in cities all around the globe and electronics manufacturers are beginning to offer repair services (although not nearly as affordable as we would like), such as iFixit, the repair and refurbish movement will continue to gain momentum.

The impact on our environment could be significant too. Electronics waste – the estimated 6.3 metric tons of waste produced globally every year – often involves toxic materials,such asmercury and lead, which can have adverse health effects on people in proximity, while harming the environment. It has been estimated that repair and refurbs could potentially save up to 50 pounds of waste per person each year according to several environmental studies.

Manufacturers are pushing back on the movement, citing that third-party repairs could cause users to harm the device, which could impact the product’s performance and potentially be an unsafe repair, however, recent legislative decisions are helping to make the repair movement a legitimate cause. New York passed theDigital Right to Repair Actearlier this month, and theEuropean Union recently passed a directive that would allow for repairers of certain electronics to be provided with spare parts from device manufacturers. While Apple continues to offer very limited repair programs, there has been an explosion of the refurbished devices market in recent years to help give consumers with budget concerns cheaper, quality alternatives to their electronic needs. Many predict that the repair and refurbish market will only continues to grow due to environmental concerns about waste and as customers’ questioning planned obsolescence practices.

The Hidden Costs of Rent Stabilization Many argue that rent stabilization programs are necessary to prevent tenants from becoming displaced. However, these policies involve significant economic tradeoffs that ultimately degrade the housing market and harm the populations they are meant to serve. Rent stabilization reduces supply, as it discourages investment and property improvements, which leads to decreased availability in the overall housing market and makes the market less affordable. 

Rent control leads to less investment in new supply and less upkeep for existing buildings because landlords cannot charge market rents. 

This contributes to a housing shortage that makes the cost of uncontrolled housing rise even faster as the stock of rent controlled housing becomes more competitive and in-demand such as New York City and San Francisco. The program also distorts the allocation of housing by creating incentives for landlords to favor existing tenants and making it difficult for new residents to gain access to housing. Some long-term renters get an enormous advantage in the housing market while new renters get little protection and face a competitive, less abundant market. Workers moving for job opportunities are discouraged by the inability to find affordable housing. 

This places those in power (long-term renters) in a better position than lower-income younger renters. 

The decline in upkeep on rent stabilized buildings is a common occurrence when costs can only be recouped by cutting expenses on building maintenance. As a result, many properties lose quality, degrading the neighborhood. Some properties are completely abandoned when the costs associated with owning the building exceed rental revenues such as in New York City. 

In the end, rent stabilization benefits a few well-positioned tenants while imposing real costs on others in the housing market. The programs tend to be inefficient ways to deliver benefits. Instead of giving below-market prices to some renters, direct financial assistance programs are a far more effective way to aid those most vulnerable to displacement. 

These programs target low-income households without stifling overall housing supply and investment. 

The basic problem is that price controls attempt to cure symptoms instead of address the root causes. More housing supply would help the problem more than price caps would because they will have the unintended consequences of decreasing the amount of housing as new supply is discouraged and what housing exists is poorly maintained, and the problem gets worse and not better.

# Community Supported Fisheries Literature Review

Community supported fisheries (CSFs) are an emerging alternative food system model that applies the principles of community supported agriculture (CSA) to fisheries and aquaculture. With a CSF, consumers can buy shares or memberships in local fishing operations in exchange for regular deliveries of catch. As the harmful impacts of industrial fishing practices become evident and demand for sustainable local foods grows among consumers, interest in CSF has surged among academics, fishers, and communities. 

The adoption of CSFs signals a growing consumer concern about where food comes from, how it is produced, and whether it supports healthy environments and equitable local communities. 

Rather than participate in production and distribution chains which mask the origins of food, consumers of CSFs engage in direct relationships with fishermen and can thus play a role in protecting marine environments.

In the CSF model, producers and consumers share risk and reward in a fishing operation. Consumers are asked to purchase a share of what a fishing operation harvests on an ongoing basis and commit to purchasing at some price before or during a fishing season. In return, they receive regular shares of the catch, along with the fishing operationâ€™s knowledge of seafood harvesting and food system sustainability issues, in exchange for that upfront payment. By reducing seafood miles in transit, increasing the resilience of small-scale fishers to the price pressures of large-scale industrial fishing, and fostering accountability among producers and consumers through shared financial and risk investment, CSFs have the potential to address many environmental and social sustainability issues.

CSFs are relatively a younger, and less studied, practice than their agricultural counterpart. While there exists an extensive body of CSA literature on CSAs Business models, environmental impacts, the CSA's and the impact of their community social impacts, the existing literature on the CSFs is more diverse, with research scattered across fields of fisheries management, sustainable food systems, and economic development. The CSF model is relative new and research on the model, though growing, only points to a vast potential for future exploration and investigation in to how these new models of food provision can contribute to sustainable food systems. 

This review summarizes and synthesizes existing literature about CSF operations, environmental sustainability in CSF operations, potential for economic Viability of CSFs, and the social benefits of CSFs, by connecting knowledge from the three key fields. 

It will identify trends in research and gaps that deserve future study.

# Asking for a Promotion After a Big Project Launches

## Wait a Beat

Give two to four weeks post-launch to let the dust settle and to have solid metrics on project performance. Don't bring it up during a crisis, or when you're manager appears frazzled or overwhelmed.

## Document Your Wins

## With concrete metrics, collect details of your contributions:

- Revenue generated or costs saved.
- Colleagues you guided or mentored.
- Problems that were solved under your own initiative.
- Any improvements in timeline or budget you delivered.

To make the case even stronger, quantify your successes: "Led the implementation team" is OK; "Led the implementation team that boosted operational efficiency by 35 percent" is better.

## Set Up a Dedicated Meeting

Don't spring this one on your boss. E-mail them requesting time to chat, with a note about the topic; something like: "I’d like to discuss my career growth and next steps; would you have about 30 minutes sometime this week to chat?" This allows your manager to prepare, and it shows the request is serious.

## Frame the Conversation

Start with enthusiasm and appreciation for the opportunity to work on the big project, and all that you learned and accomplished. Then transition gracefully to the request; consider something along the lines of: "I’ve greatly enjoyed contributing to this team and I'm so proud of what we've accomplished. Because of that, I'm interested in taking on more responsibility and would like to explore the possibility of promotion into [mention target job title]."

## Build Your Case

Articulate how you've contributed beyond the expected parameters of your current role and why you're ready for a move up:
- Your consistent history of good performance.
- Any new skills or abilities gained in the role.
- Leadership or management opportunities you've taken on.
- Growth beyond your original role's scope.

## Prepare for Q&A and Listen

Your manager may respond immediately with an acceptance, a "no," or "we need to discuss timelines." If they're non-committal, be direct: "What would I need to do or demonstrate to earn this promotion?"

## Follow-Up in Writing

Once the meeting is done, send an e-mail that sums up key discussion points, decisions made and any agreements on next steps or performance metrics. This will serve as an excellent reference.

## If You Don't Get It This Time

If the answer is no, ask when you can discuss this again. More importantly, find out what you’ll need to do to be considered for a promotion in the future. Then make sure to deliver! Promotions are awarded for performance, and your project experience is your proof points.

# 10 Tips for Better Home Audio on a Budget

Who says you need a stadium budget to experience concert-hall sound at home? It doesn’t have to break the bank to make your living room a sonic sanctuary. Here’s how:

1. Placement is key. Don't buy a thing before you try re-arranging your existing speakers. Corners and walls enhance bass, while center placement often leads to the clearest sound.

2. Soften things up. 

##  That cozy blanket, heavy curtains, and thick rug?

They're also sound dampeners. 

The free solution to annoying echoes and reflections.

3. Get a good Bluetooth speaker. Modern wireless technology means great sound doesn’t always come with a hefty wire price tag.

4. Upgrade your music source. Bad input = bad output. Even using a streaming service like Tidal that offers lossless audio quality can make a difference over standard MP3s.

5. Get a modest amplifier. If your speakers are older, an affordable little amp can be a game changer. You can find decent ones for under $100 nowadays.

6. Scope out vintage and second-hand audio equipment. If you’re patient, you can find amazing deals on Craigslist or Facebook Marketplace. Used high-quality speakers often sound far better than their budget new counterparts, and cost a fraction of the price.

7. Build DIY acoustic panels. If you’re handy, make simple panels by covering a framework of rigid foam or mineral wool insulation with fabric. This will kill sound reflections just as effectively as their far more expensive commercial counterparts.

8. Dust your components. It sounds crazy, but dirt and dust build-up in your components and drivers can degrade sound quality over time.

9. Ensure your cables are decent. Quality interconnect and speaker cables can affect sound, but you don’t need anything too expensive to improve upon very cheap cables that may cause interference.

10. Address your room. None of the equipment in the world can compensate for a bad-sounding room! The biggest bang-for-your-buck improvement will come from controlling reflections and minimizing echoes-using placement, furniture and soft furnishings.

Basically, smart is always better than expensive! Just take it one step at a time.

# The Limits of Regulating Facial Recognition

Facial recognition technology, is no exception and too much regulation might stunt its legitimate potential at a societal level and through regulatory inefficiencies strike back on public security and innovation itself.

The idea that more regulations can control technology demonstrates a deep misunderstanding of how the tech world works. We have, for example, facial recognition deployed worldwide in countries with wildly varying legal regimes. A heavy-handed ban in one area simply pushes development to another place where oversight is even looser. Excess regulation protects incumbents, not citizens; it imposes compliance costs that only established corporates can bear and leave criminals and authoritarian states free to act without constraint.

In addition, regulation is having a very hard time keeping up with fast-paced technology. When lawmakers write laws to regulate current capabilities, by those timelines the tech has already moved on. Restrictive policies become outdated long before they are revised and constantly need to be updated. This generates legal ambiguity that stifles legitimate innovation in places where facial recognition has real benefit, such as airport security, locating missing children, and tracking criminals.

The justification on which most regulatory pressure rests â€” privacy concerns â€” are legitimate but often overstated. In fact, the existing legal frameworks already cover the main concerns: warrant requirements, data protection laws and anti-discrimination statutes. Such tools can manage facial recognition well, without the need for specialized legislation that may prove to be counterproductive by doing more harm than good by limiting promising applications.

Context matters enormously. The use of facial recognition at a border checkpoint presents quite different risks than deployment in retail stores. However, that broad regulation often applies a one-size-fits-all approach that places either overly burdensome restrictions on appropriate uses of the technology or fails to provide adequate protections when necessary. Clear sectoral action beats high-level categorical bans

Instead of working with restrictive regulation, we can move directly to the solutions offered by transparency and accountability mechanisms. Documentation of systems' error rates and demographic-wide accuracy, as well as how they will be used, would permit policymakers to provide oversight without imposing one-size-fits-all bans. Self-regulation in the industry combined with narrowly tailored legal remedies directly tying to real, proven harms provides flexibility to address legitimate concerns while protecting innovation.

There are significant advantages that facial recognition brings to humans. Yes, having safeguards in place is required, but over-regulating AI implementation will not hit a bull's eye. More intelligent methodsâ€”transparent implementation, targeted limitation and already available legal structuresâ€”strike a far better balance between encouraging innovation and an individual sense of safety.

A Literature Review: Youth Sports Specialization, Childhood Burnout

The youth sports milieu has changed dramatically over the past 20 years with a growing focus on early specialization and high levels of competitive sport-specific training (Jayanthi et al., 2015). Sports specialization, defined as the year-round, high-intensity training in a single sport starting at an early age, among youth athletes has increased in prevalence due to parental/personal aspirations, social pressures, and expectations societally that elite status can only be achieved through commitment earlier than ever before (Côté & Vierimaa, 2014). Nevertheless, this trend has occurred alongside mounting concern about athlete burnout, a multidimensional syndrome defined by emotional exhaustion, reduced sense of accomplishment and sport devaluation (Raedeke & Smith, 2001).

Young athletes are at risk of burnout, which Eime and others (2013) have described as an area of serious public health concern, with preliminary data suggesting prevalence rates between 10% and 40%, depending on the sport and the sex/age group studied (Gould et al., 1996). The interplay of early specialization and burnout however may be an area in extreme need of further study as initiating athletes to specialized training at a young age may subject developing athletes to chronic stress and overtraining, as well as psychological factors that fundamentally rob them from finding enjoyment and continuity with sport.

The literature has identifyied competing frameworks: single-sport specialization models that emphasize deliberate practice and skill development, versus multi-sport participation models that emphasize holistic development and intrinsic motivation (Baker et al., 2003). Although some studies back up that early specialization is one of the roads to achievement, there are now indications that this path may involve psychological costs (Ericsson et al., 1993; Stryer et al., 2000), especially in terms of burnout.

Objective To compile and summarize recent evidence across studies exploring the relationship between youth sports specialization on burnout. This review intends to clarify the specialization practices as a risk factor for childhood burnout and elucidate the protective mechanisms that may reduce maladaptive psychological outcomes among youth athletes based on empirical findings, theoretical frameworks, and contextual factors impacting this relationship.

# 16-Week Century Training Guide

## Weeks 1-4: Base Building
Step 1: Ride Easy and Set a Base. Aim for 3-4 rides per week, at easy conversational pace – Make your longer training ride reach 40–50 miles by week four. Add a hill workout once a week to build strength. Steady effort is more important than intensity and it provides the base from which injuries are prevented.

## Weeks 5-8: Endurance Development
Forum Marque Maintain frequency of Riding sessions at 4–5 per week. Your longest ride should be between 60 and 75 miles. Include a tempo ride (steady effort for sustained time) and hill repeat session. Fueling strategies: start practicing it on long rides — try different gels, bars and drinks to see what works in your stomach.

## Weeks 9-12: Peak Building
Continue doing 4-5 rides a week, with one being 80 to 90 miles. Schedule Isolation Cardio to Develop Speed and Power Train on long hills at race pace. Practice your nutrition plan on similar terrain — ride until you can no longer reproduce the slightest motion of riding, simulating race conditions.

This is the same speed with which most of you will finish your marathon.
Decrease mileage by 30-40% with low intensity 50-60 Miles as your long ride so far. Prioritise recovery with enough sleep, stretching and massage. Do a recap of how you tackled the pacing, with the first half being slower than the second.

## Week 16: Race Week
Make rides short and light (20-30 miles at a time). 2-3 days before the event you rest totally. Tick your gear, nutrition and plan. Prepare your Support Items and check the bike one last time.

## General Tips
- Rest one full day each week
- Hydrate and fuel properly
- Pay attention to your body—take more rest days as necessary
- Increase mileage gradually (by no more than 10% each week)
- Due to continue sailing on a terrain similar to that of your century

It's worth noting that pure fitness isn't the only relevant aspect—how you approach and pace yourself in these events, along with your fueling habits and mental processes. Start conservative and finish strong.

Windowsills can get *hot*. The temperature could get high enough in summer to put your plants under stress. Good air circulation helps.

Autoplay features and on-purpose media habits

The way autoplay is designed blatantly subverts the desire to actively engage with media. This makes passive consumption the path of least resistance as these mechanisms automatically skip to another episode, video or song, reducing the friction between finishing a piece of content and starting it again.

When users have to actively choose what to do next, they create a decision point—a moment of hesitation where they can ask themselves if they really want to proceed. Autoplay eliminates this cognitive checkpoint. Do I want to start another episode? Users have to purposely break the cycle of automatic advancement. The fact that this burden of proof has effectively been reversed drastically changes the behavior. Studies on default settings show that anything requiring no effort gets disproportionately high usage—whether its decided utility tracks with a user preference or not.

Autoplay also exploits psychological vulnerabilities. This is the very principle that teaches us about the mere exposure effect; we subscribe to content and it starts seeming so much better each time. Moreover, the initiation of new content has an activation energy which, when it occurs automatically, acts as a trigger for "binge drift": consuming far more than was initially planned.

However, autoplay isn't entirely problematic. It makes things more convenient for passive activities like background music or everyday commutes. It becomes a problem when autoplay is the default for things that need focused and thinking.

This is runway key difference comes down to the context. Autoplay for instrumental music works differently than autoplaying narrative drive shows where people lose all track of time. These platforms can offer a little more moderation by providing per-content type autoplay toggle or requiring users to periodically re-confirm their engagement.

Both autoplay features and automatic recommendations, really make it harder to build intentional habits (especially with complex media). Regaining intentionality either requires platforms to redesign defaults, or for users to intentionally turn off those features—though the latter involves way more work than any technological design should require.

A Literature Review: Public Transit funding in growing suburb

Urbanization and suburbanization of metropolitan areas across North America and the globe is happening at a pace never seen before, leading to challenges in developing and maintaining transit infrastructure. The growth of populations in suburbs has increased the need for more accessible, reliable public transportation, but funding mechanisms have not kept up with this expansion. In suburban contexts public transit has some very different attributes from the urban systems, being less dense, instead characterized by more dispersed development patterns and a reliance on commuters using their own cars for transport. As a result, suburbs have received a disproportionate share of transit investment when compared to their growing population.

The funding challenges for suburban transit systems are different than the problems metropolitan areas face with traditional urban transit. In conventional terms, revenue sources including farebox collections, local taxes, and state grants are frequently insufficient to cover the relatively high cost of operating in areas with lower density and smaller ridership bases. More recent more scholarly work looks at alternative financing strategies that have emerged such as public–private partnerships, developer exactions, congestion pricing and regional finance. Climate change concerns and remote work trends are also accelerating policy debates around where transit investment dollars can be best spent.

Competing views on the best funding models emerge from the literature. Regional coordination paired with geographically pooled funding is recommended by some researchers as a strategy to allocate resources equitably across suburban systems. Others emphasize the importance of local control and solutions suited to individual suburban contexts. The degree of support for suburban transit investment capacity through federal and state policy frameworks is even more heterogeneous at the jurisdictional level.

While there is a growing recognition of how transit can help serve suburban development sustainably, we still lack much comparative knowledge on which funding tools are most effective in different suburban contexts. This review compiles contemporary research on suburban transit funding, including sources of funds, innovative policies, and outcomes. This review synthesizes existing literature to better understand contemporary challenges facing funding and promising practices that may assist transit development in growing suburban communities.

## Getting Started

Begin by identifying interested neighbors. Do things like put up fliers, send emails, or mention it in conversation. Target 6 –12 members and this is a comfortable size for dialogue but not too big.

Pick a monthly or biweekly meeting schedule. Set a regular time, place: at someone's home, like a coffee shop or library.

## Selecting Books

Employ a democratic method: members propose titles and the next choice is decided by vote. Keep the genres fresh; Try different ones. Pay attention to the length and complexity of a book: books roughly 200–300 pages long are comfortable for most groups to read. Provide sufficient reading time for meetings (generally 4-6 weeks).

## Structuring Meetings

Start every session providing refreshments to create a sense of community. Dedicate 60-90 minutes for discussion. Open your review with the broad strokes then pull focus to themes, characters and writing style. Help the quiet members to say what they wish.

Be clear about what is required from the above-mentioned positions for all meetings so that discussions can be kept focused.

## Keeping Momentum

Rotate hosting to even things out. Integrate popular fiction, classics and obscure books that will widen members' horizons. Invite a local author or librarian to talk occasionally.

Take away: You know your kids — note right about attendance — set expectations for what participation looks like. Check in with anyone who misses meetings too frequently.

## Sustaining Interest

Break it up every once in a while: Have themed potlucks, go to author events or arrange video calls with authors. Use Goodreads to curate an online shared reading list Honor milestones — the anniversary of your club, for example.

Keep in mind that people join book clubs for community as much as literature. Be genuinely friends by not only conversing but also being with each other.

## Handling Challenges

If there are disputes about book choices, encourage members of the group by reminding them that reading different viewpoints will enrich discussions. If it feels like the group is going through a dry spell, poll members to see what they'll be interested in, and adapt.

The Ethics of AI-Generated Artwork in Children's Books

The use of AI-generated artwork in children's books raises complex ethical questions that must be carefully considered.

**Arguments for** hinge on accessibility and efficiency. Graphic-designed AI and the implementation of text-to-image tools will streamline the production process, allowing  companies with a smaller defined audience to make books like illustrated children's books at an affordable cost. Others might democratize illustration for independent authors who lack the budget to bring in professional artists.

**However, significant concerns exist. At first, there is the problem of artist payment and job displacement. AI systems are trained on pre-existing artwork—often without express consent or compensation to original artists. Professional illustrators in a market sector where human creativity has long­ been highly valued (although poorly compensated), will lose out on work, including clients unwilling and/or unable to invest in costly AI technologies.

Second, illustrating children's books is pedagogically loaded. The illustrations set up for children how they will interpret representation, beauty and diversity. Because these AI systems are trained on pre-existing data, it is possible that they may replicate the historical biases found in representations of race, gender and ability.

The third is authenticity and values. Children's literature has historically emphasised that human creators have connections of value with young readers. AI artwork disrupts this interrelation and might lower the cultural significance of a book.

Possible ethical paths forward might involve transparency requirements: with clear labels that these illustrations were created by AI and thus informing the reader of how this book was made. Publishers would also be wise to commit to hybrid approaches—augmenting rather than replacing human artists with AI tools, or guaranteeing fair compensation if and when professional work is included in training data.

Long story short, AI Art in Kidlit is not immoral as long as it is done correctly. Innovation needs to be balanced with respect for artists, child development, and a commitment to meaningful representation. Succumbing to the lure of convenient AI will prove detrimental if done without those safeguards.

Does Rent Stabilization Come at a Cost?

Rent stabilization is intended to protect tenants from displacement, but it comes at an enormous economic cost that ultimately worsens conditions in the housing market and threatens those precise households most at risk.

Property investment and maintenance are discouraged as rent controls limit availability. When landlords cannot set rents to market levels, it helps grease the wheels for even less construction of new housing or upgrading existing units. The availability of supply is restricted, which further raises prices on unregulated markets and ironically makes house more unaffordable overall. This is the case in cities such as San Francisco and New York: stringent rent control => larger average rents, as the rare stock which is affordable become ever more sought-after.

Such programs skew the allocation of housing as well. The stabilization of the units becomes a luxury good and leads to perverse incentives. Long-term tenants get insulating perks but a new generation of citizens — often youthful and working-class — find the walkways blocked. That limits labour mobility, as workers are reluctan t to move for jobs when finding affordable housing is impossible. The theory seems to be the policy to help the poor actually favors those who already have housing.

Building improvements cannot occur if the rental income does not cover maintenance costs. Landlords these days are concerned only with cutting costs, and if there is this continuous deterioration of a property over time, it will eventually degrade the quality of the neighborhood. Others let properties fall into total disrepair when operating costs aren't covered by regulated income, exacerbating the shortage of available housing.

In addition, rent stabilization is focused on narrowly defined benefits. The lucky few have artificially low rents while imposing negative externalities on the rest of us. That represented a relatively inefficient form of redistribution compared with direct assistance programs targeting low-income renters, targeting without distorting the broader housing market.

Price control is put in place to treat symptoms, not causes. At the core, a better answer is to boost housing supply by easing zoning norms, lowering construction restrictions, and simplifying development approval methods. These methods broaden access while avoiding the pitfalls of controlled shortages.

Rent stabilization is a misguided policy moving in the wrong direction. In reducing supply and misallocating housing, however, these programs both harm the populations they purport to help and create persistent economic inefficiencies. Solutions that expand supply and are more effectively targeted at those most in need have shown better success empirically.

# Literature Review: Community-Supported Fisheries

Community-supported fisheries (CSF) are a new model of local food systems that adapt community-supported agriculture (CSA) to marine and freshwater. This model involves consumers who buy shares or memberships in local fishing operations, paying for a member's financial stake and assuming a risk share of the catch over time. With increasing awareness of industrial fishing methods and their sustainability issues in food systems, seafood community resilience has become an area of both research and practice, with Community Supported Fisheries (CSF) considered a promising approach to more just and sustainable seafood production-and-distribution.

CSFs point to wider changes in consumer awareness around the origins of their food, sustainable practices and support for local economies. Unlike traditional supply chains, which often may not be clear about who the producers and consumers are, CSF is built on value transparency, meaningful relationships between producers and consumers of climate stewardship goods & services, and collective responsibility for environmental stewardship. Multi-dimensional in that it addresses sustainable seafood distribution carbon footprint reduction, small scale fishers facing industrial competition for buyers and responsible harvest practice consumer awareness and involvement to name a few.

Yet CSF continues to be overlooked compared to its agricultural counterpart. Although CSA literature is voluminous and typically topic-driven (i.e. business models (BM), environmental outcomes (EO), or social impacts(SI)) CSF scholarship is dispersed across many fields, such as fisheries management, sustainable food systems, and economic development fields. This variety is a testament to the relative youth of CSF, as both an activity and research topic. Existing research offers hope but also identifies key barriers, including the challenges related to this catch variability, logistical difficulties and building consumer trust in new species and sustainable supply.

This literature review synthesizes established research regarding community-supported fisheries, the structural workings of their operations, claims of environmental sustainability and economic viabilityâ€“all while reaping social benefits. This review synthesises insights from fisheries science, food systems scholarship and community development to discover key themes, research gaps and opportunities for future exploration of this emerging food system model.

# Asking For a Raise After You Ship A Big Project

## Timing Is Everything

After launching their project, wait two to four weeks. It gives stakeholders a chance to evaluate results and let the dust settle. Do not ask during a crisis mode, or when your manager is also stressed.

## Build Your Case

Record your impact with measurable metrics:
â€“ Revenue created or expenses avoided
- Team members you mentored
- Problems you solved independently
- Improved Timeline or Budget that you launched

Quantify impact whenever possible. Weak: "Led implementation." Stronger: "Led implementation that increased operational efficiency by 35%.

## Schedule a Formal Conversation

Don't ambush your manager. Write them an email: "Hey, I would like to talk about my career vision and next steps. Got 30 minutes to spare this week?" It provides them with some time to prepare and indicates that you are a professional.

## Structure the Discussion

To begin with, you should share honest excitement about this project succeeding as well as how your position connects to it. Then flow into your promotion ask-

I've enjoyed being part of this group, and I'm proud of what we achieved. "I think the time is right for me to take on more responsibility, and I would like you to consider me for a promotion to [position title].

## Present Your Value Proposition

Explain why you deserve promotion:
- Consistent performance track record
- New skills developed
- Leadership capabilities demonstrated
- How you have grown out of your job

## Listen and Respond

Your manager could respond by saying, yes, no or "let's talk about timeline." If they stall, straight out ask: "What do I need to show on these factors to get promoted? Get specific, actionable feedback.

## Follow Up in Writing

Write a follow up email about what you talked about and what the next steps are. This creates accountability and documentation.

## Handle Rejection Gracefully

If the answer is no, ask when you will be able to bring it up again. Call out criteria for preservation and have your promise to meet it.

Remember: promotions reward demonstrated performance. The best argument you have is your success on the projectâ€”use it wisely.

# Youth Sports Specialization and Childhood Burnout: A Literature Review

The sports scene for youth has rapidly changed the past two decades, with increased early specialization and training (Jayanthi et al., 2015). Specialization in youth sport is an early commitment to the single sport training year round with the goal of achieving sporting expertise (Côté & Vierimaa, 2014). Specialization has become more apparent in younger athletes due to the aspirations of parents, pressure from society, and perceived need to specialize to achieve sporting excellence (Côté & Vierimaa, 2014). The increased specialization of youth sport has caused concern for athlete burnout, which is a complex combination of emotional exhaustion, a lack of satisfaction, and the devaluation of sport (Raedeke & Smith, 2001).

The burnout of young athletes is a public health problem, as preliminary research shows burnout occurs in 10-40% of young athletes based on sport and age group (Gould et al., 1996). Specialization and burnout must be researched to identify the cause and effect relationship because specialization exposes young athletes to chronic burnout and overtraining. Specialization has the potential to consume athletes and cause burnout and devaluation of sport.

Based on the literature, the framework around single specialization of youth sport training vs. training of sport for youth (Baker et al., 2003) shows the trade-off between achieving sporting excellence and the potential negative psychological effects of early specialization. Emerging psychology research shows early specialization can delay the potential for sporting burnout, as athletes stray from the original reason of their sporting participation (Stryer et al., 2000).

This literature review synthesizes existing research on youth sports specialization and burnout. This review analyzes empirical research, theories, and contextual factors to answer the question of whether there is a meaningful relationship between early sports specialization and childhood burnout. This review also aims to identify factors that may shield young athletes from the adverse psychological effects of sport specialization.

# 16-Week Century Training Guide

## Base Building – Weeks 1-4

Work your way up to 3-4 rides per week. This week designate your rides to easy conversation pace efforts. Complete one hill strength training workout every week. By the end of the fourth week work your way up to a 40-50 mile long ride.

## Weeks 5-8 Endurance Development

Begin your week building 4-5 rides. Work your longest ride to 60-75 miles the first part of the week, and begin incorporating your first tempo workouts (consistent hard efforts) and interval training. You also will want to begin incorporating Hill Repeat workouts

and also start your first efforts at fueling workouts to determine what forms aid you can tolerate for the longest time.

## Peak Building Weeks 9-12

Reduce your training rides to 4-5 rides per week. Works one of your rides to 80-90 miles. Begin incorporating paces efforts for hill workouts and train your efforts at pacing at race pace for longer climbing efforts.

## Weeks 13-15

Re-zero your training by reducing your weekly miles by 30-40 percent. This week maintain your intensity efforts, works longer 50-60 mile rides. Concentrate on recovery by increasing your sleep efforts and stretching and massaging.

## Race Season Week 16

Keep your efforts short and easy for the first two rides of the week. Take 2-3 days off before your competition. Ride your planned route and test your nutrition and equipment. Be sure to check your bike for last minute adjustments.

## General Tips 

- Take at least one day off training every week.

- Avoid dehydration and poor nutrition.

- Take off more days than you think you need.

- Slowly increase overall distance trained by 10% each week. 

- Practice training on similar terrain to your century ride.

The most important aspects are pacing, feeding yourself, and mental preparation. Go slow at the beginning, and go fast at the end.

# Intentional Mindset and Media Autoplay

Features designed for frictionless media consumption fly in the face of intentional media consumption. You can think of automatic media consumption features as removing the barrier of having to choose what you want to consume next. Passive consumption becomes the easiest option. 

If you have to choose the next thing you want to consume, you are forced to pause and decide whether you want to continue consuming media. Autoplay eliminates a cognitive checkpoint by forcing you to interrupt automatic progression to determine whether you want to watch another episode. 

Defaults behave similarly to Autoplay features. Whatever requires the least amount of action tends to get used the most regardless of how it conflicts with user preferences.

Autoplay relies on the mere exposure effect. Consuming media through autoplay makes you like it and lose track of time, making it easy to consume way more media than intended.

In many cases, Autoplay is harmless. Media consumption features designed for passive activities are easy to use and convenient. The concern becomes when intention based activities begin using Autoplay as a central feature.

The distinction relies on context. Autoplay for passive, simplistic background content differs from Autoplay for media that drives engagement. Balancing user autonomy and convenience may require content Autoplay features to be opt in on an activity basis.

Autoplay features make it difficult to build intentional habits for complex media. Building intentional habits either requires a thoughtful redesign of defaults by the platform or the user actively disabling the feature. The latter should not require much effort on the userâ€™s part.

Unintentional habits are easy to build with complex media when paired with autoplay features. The passive viewing that may come from using autoplay features would not be intentional. Building intention requires a user to consciously decide to enable and disable features. The development of good habits also requires some level of intention.

# Hybrid Learning Changes the Shape of University Lecture Halls

Blended in-person and online learning models, known as hybrid learning, are altering traditional class designs at universities around the world. They offer students new choices on the pathways they take through their education.

The changes took off during the pandemic, but many are here to stay. Instead of replacing traditional lectures, universities are using new models that let students attend classes virtually and offer recorded lectures that can be accessed at any time.

"The lecture hall is transforming," said Dr. Sarah Chen, an educational technology researcher at Cambridge University. Rather than focusing on traditional methods of delivering content to students, "the reality is that students may not even be present," she said.

Recorded lectures have been game changing for many students, especially international students who have to deal with time zone differences.

While many universities take the recordings of lectures for granted, some have argued that the change has diminished the value of the university experience. Solely relying on recorded lectures may mean students miss many of the teachable moments on campus that come from impromptu discussions among the students and faculty. According to Professor James Mitchell of Oxford University, "there is a real risk of creating a two-tier system where remote students receive diminished educational experiences."

According to university leaders, the post-pandemic future will likely include face-to-face lectures, but there will be use of technology to support learning. There will be more recorded lectures, but there will still be in-person seminars and lab sessions.

The recovery from the pandemic offers an opportunity for universities to use the flexibility that hybrid learning provides without a complete commitment to online learning. Changes to larger classroom lectures will likely be welcomed and may be integrated more widely, but the core of what it means to have the lecture hall experience will not change.

# Newsletter Writers as Trusted Commentators

Newsletter writers have become some of the most credible sources of commentary in our increasingly distrusting world. Unlike traditional media outlets, newsletter writers are more concerned about maintaining trust through actual authentic behavior and self-accountability rather than serving clicks.

Many newsletter writers have better relationships with their audience than most media outlets. Readers willingly subscribe to newsletters, allowing for tangible communication and a feedback system. This continues to incentivize accuracy over media outlets that have lost trust and gatekeepers.

Their increasing popularity is not a failing of information consumption, but audiences deliberating whom they place their trust in.

# Public Transit Funding in Growing Suburbs: A Literature Review

North American and international suburban and metropolitan regions are growing rapidly, placing a strain on the design and maintenance of transport infrastructure. Growth of the suburbs creates more demand for convenient and reliable public transport. Public transport funding projects also grow as suburban populations grow. Providing public transport for suburban areas is also very different from providing it for urban spaces. Suburban growth patterns, cultural preferences, development styles and population distribution favor the use of private vehicles for commuting over public transport. Because suburban areas have grown over the years but have been underfunded, the suburbs have almost no public transport systems.

There are various differences in funding public transport in the suburbs from funding public transport in urban spaces. Reduced population densities and longer commuting distances mean that suburban areas are more costly to serve than urban areas. For many years, funding public suburban transport meant lower revenues, local taxes, and state aid. However, many scholars are advocating for new kinds of funding systems such as public-private partnerships, developer transport exactions, congestion charging, and regional funds.

The literature looks at funding public suburban transport and does not give a single, final answer to the best way to fund public suburban transport. Even so, some scholars have focused on regional equitable funding and coordinated transport systems. Other scholars have focused on local and communityriven solutions for public suburban transport. Variable support for suburban transport from the federal and state governments limits the capacity of transport systems in suburban areas.

While more people recognize the role of transit in designing sustainable suburbs, important findings are still missing for different kinds of suburbs on which funding mechanisms work best. This study looks at suburban transit financing, looks at funding sources and policy innovations and measures what they achieved. By looking at what has already been written, this study tries to find out where the obstacles to funding are now and what has proven to be useful in supporting transit development in suburbs.

# How to Begin and Sustain a Neighborhood Book Club

## Beginnings

It helps to find out who is interested first. Flyers, emails and even discussions are great ways to gather interested participants. Shoot for 6-12 members. This size should work for a good discussion without it getting out of control.

The first step is to pick a consistent meeting day and time each month or every other week. You can set the meeting place to be the same or rotate it. A coffee shop or library would be good places, but someone’s house would work too.

## Voting Time

A democratic process is the easiest when it comes to picking books. Members suggest books, then a club vote decides the selection. It is also good to have a variety of genres. When it comes to the length of a book, 200-300 pages works well for most groups. With a voting system, it is good to give people time to read the book after voting for it since that may take a few weeks.

## Discussion Time

Like other things, it is important to have a good community to get the ball rolling. Bringing snacks to meetings in the 60-90 minute time frame is good and can be a starter for discussions. It is good to get many things out of the way to allow for a discussion on the impressions, theme, character, and the style of the writing. Good book clubs enjoy having their quiet members speak.

## Leading the Meeting

The discussion should be focused and guided without allowing the meeting to get off track. This should be the responsibility of the discussion leader.

## Passing the Responsibility

A good, easy way to pass the responsibility of hosting is to let that person be the discussion leader. This ensures a good and focused meeting.

## Keeping Up with Members

A book club dies off easy. To keep members involved it is good to mix up the book selections. Local authors and librarians make great guest speakers for book club meetings. Out of concern for members who are not attending regularly, it would be good practice to follow up with them.

## Keeping the Interest Alive

Good book clubs enjoy good variety. Some good examples can be themed potlucks, author events can be good meeting replacements, and author video calls/meetings can be fun. Goodreads is a good website to use. It allows members to keep track of the various books they read, and to keep the reader’s list organized. Good book clubs celebrate their successes. That could be a new anniversary.

People need to live their social lives outside the book club. Social groups formed between members have the potential to be genuine friendships.

## Finding Solutions

Disagreements about book selections can be resolved by suggesting that different opinions lead to more interesting discussions. The group can feel stagnate, and if that happens, it is probably time to experiment with new interests.

A book club is easy to start and the potential outcome is a lasting connection with members and your community and appreciation for a variety of works of literature.

Consumers empower the Right to Repair movement by repairing or refurbishing devices instead of discarding them, challenging the throwaway culture dominant in the tech industry.

# The Economic Costs of Rent Stabilization

Tenant advocates cite rent stabilization as an important protection from the threat of displacement; however, these policies impose significant costs on the market and the economy as a whole.

First, rental control dampens market-related investments in property and eventually diminishes upkeep of property. If landlords are not able to earn market rate returns, then there is even less incentive to undertake new construction and/or renovation of existing properties. As the supply of property dwindles, demand for housing in unregulated markets increases, driving an across-the-board increase of housing costs. As the example of New York City and San Francisco demonstrates, market rents increase as the supply of rent controlled units becomes more competitive. Rent stabilization eventually pushes the market costs higher.

Stabilized rent units create dislocations in the housing market. Tenants who gain long-term rental agreements have advantages that newer, generally lower income, and younger tenants do not have. This creates barriers to new, much needed, labor mobility.

Rent control encourages landlords to abandon rental units, as the costs of upkeep become greater than the economic returns from rented units. This decreases the supply of housing and worsens the quality of the neighborhood.

Finally, while a small group of tenants benefits from the lower rents, a much larger group potentially suffers from the market distortions caused from rent controls. Rent stabilization is an inefficient tool for providing housing subsidies.

# Literature Review: Community-Supported Fisheries

The concept of community-supported fisheries (CSF) is built on the community-supported agriculture (CSA) model and is a new food system model focused primarily on marine and freshwater fisheries. With CSF, customers buy shares or memberships to a local fishing operation and assume some of the financial risk. In return, customers receive regular harvested fish. As concern around the sustainability of industrial fishing and the sustainability of the food system and the resilience of the surrounding communities grow, so too has the interest and focus on the CSF model and how it can support holistic and sustainable approaches to both seafood harvest and the harvest of other resources.

CSF is responsive to shifts in modern consumer culture because it focuses on the end consumers and fishermen, and it addresses the sustainability challenges of harvested resources (fish) while also limiting the potential environmental impact of harvested resources transport. Additionally, because CSF addresses the financial challenges faced by small-scale fishermen and of fishing operations, it also serves the goal of responsible fishing. 

Compared to the growing literature on community-supported agriculture, CSF is an emerging field of study. Unlike CSA, there is no well-defined body of literature examining CSF and its business models. Existing fragmented literature is found across fisheries management, sustainable food systems, and economic development. The main focus of these publications is the potential of CSF as opposed to the challenges such as variability of catches, logistical challenges, and consumer acceptance of changing supplies and unfamiliar species.

This review integrates existing literature on community-supported fisheries (CSFs) to better understand their operational structures, environmental sustainability claims, economic viability, and asserted social value. To accomplish this reviewâ€™s goal, perspectives from fisheries science, the food system, and community development have been combined. Through this combination, key themes, as well as barriers and limits to research and their corresponding opportunities, have been identified and described.

# Here's How You Should Ask For a Promotion After Having Shipped That Big Project

## Timing is Key

Consider waiting for two to four weeks after the launch of the project. You want to give time for the dust to settle, and stakeholders to analyze and evaluate their findings. Further, you would not want to approach your manager during a crisis. Wait for the appropriate time. 

## Your Case for the Promotion

You need documentation detailing your contribution for this promotion, and you should use quantifiable metrics:

- Revenue generated, costs saved

- Team members mentored

- Independent resolution of issues

- Improvement of timelines or budgets

Metrics should be used to outline the impact of your work. “Led implementation” should be amended to “Led implementation of the project that improved efficiency by 35%.”

## Book Your 30 Minute Slot to Discuss

You do not want to catch your manager off guard. Use the following language to book a time: “I’d like to discuss my career growth and next steps. Do you have 30 minutes this week?”  This shows your consideration of their time, and that you are prepared for your discussion.

## Structure the Discussion

Begin by showing your excitement for the team's project success. Then lead into your request for promotion:

"It has been a pleasure contributing to the team. I am glad to see the results of our effort. I have built up my confidence to the extent that I think I can take on more and request a promotion to [specific role]."

## Present Your Value Proposition

Describe why you should be promoted:

- Consistent performance

- New skills

- Leadership

- Forecasted growth beyond current role

## Listen and Respond

Expect your manager to either say yes, say no, or say "let's discuss timing." If they give you a "maybe" answer, don't be afraid to ask "what have I not demonstrated that would earn this promotion?" Be clear and concise on the off chance they actually give you feedback.

## Follow Up in Writing

Message them showing you took the time to listen after the meeting to the agreement on next steps.

## Handling Rejection

If denied, wait for another opportunity to discuss it, and ask for clear, specific guidelines on how to better improve on what was lacking with your previous request.

Keep in mind promotions are results driven. Your success on this project should be your best reasoning tool.

# The Modern Day Issue: Inbox Overload

Inbox overload has become a modern day problem with several factors combining and converging in the digital age. First, because email is so accessible and has a very low barrier to entry, people send messages quickly and at any time with, sometimes, little to no concern. This creates a culture of excessive emailing, with people sending messages to large groups and even sending non-time sensitive messages.

Compounding this is the ‘always on’ culture. With smartphones and notifications, employees feel the need to check their emails all the time. Now messages that would have been consolidated into one daily communication are sent throughout the day and night, creating fragmented attention.

Add to this the failures of organizational communication. Many businesses do not set clear guidelines for the uses of each form of communication, and as a result employees rely on email to the point of over communication for everything from a quick message to a message that should be conveyed in a meeting or an instant message.

Furthermore, the number of automated messages an individual receives on a daily basis has grown significantly. Notifications from systems, newsletters, advertisements, automated messages, and updates are all sent to employees’ inboxes.

These issues are also a result of a lack of organizational culture around best practices for email use. Virtually every employee is someone who has grown up in the digital age with virtually all employees lacking early generation filing systems and strategies for managing large tasks/messages.

The desire to respond quickly to all emails creates stress and anxiety. Employees have adopted a mindset that email is a synchronous communication method instead of an asynchronous one.

Fixing inbox overload requires organizational changes including new policies and guidelines for email communication, automated mechanisms for flexible message type classification and filtering, cultural norms for focusing attention, and reducing unwarranted message distribution and notification delivery.

It is a challenging task to resolve inbox overload. One main reason for this is the nature of tasks required to resolve inbox overload.

# Older neighborhoods prepare for the electric vehicle revolution

Older residential neighborhoods have begun preparing for the electric vehicle revolution largely in response to the challenges associated with their age and infrastructure. 

Newer residential communities built with advanced energy systems, like dedicated parking spaces, have the ability to quickly accommodate the residents’ needs as new technologies and or vehicles come to market. Older communities lack this infrastructure. 

As a result, many community members end up using street parking and outdated electric systems that were designed to serve much lower energy demands.

“We're seeing a real infrastructure gap,” says Maria Chen. “Homeowners without driveways can't easily install private chargers, and many cities haven't yet deployed sufficient public charging stations.” 

Several cities are beginning to create more equity and accessibility to EV charging. Portland Metro for example, is installing 50 public charging stations in underserved communities. New York City has also launched a program to install EV chargers in apartment buildings.  

Accessibility and equity to EV charging technologies often requires community partnerships. In Boston, the EV Access Initiative works to develop optimal spaces to install new charging systems. 

 EV charging technology creates many financial concerns for older communities. Each charging unit costs thousands to install and communities must upgrade the dated technologies and electrical systems. In addition, residents are concerned with the aesthetics and safety of street charging systems.

Advocates remain hopeful in the face of challenges. James Rodriguez, a transportation analyst, says, “These neighborhoods have our most diverse and walkable communities. Prioritizing the installation of EV charging here is environmentally necessary and socially equitable.”

For communities to successfully transition to an EV driven future without leaving certain communities behind is how the equity and climate crisis goals will be met.

# Youth Sports Specialization and Childhood Burnout: A Literature Review

Massive changes have taken place in the sphere of youth sports in the past twenty years, which reflect the growing interest in early specialization and training (Jayanthi et al., 2015). Sport specialization has become commonly practiced by young athletes, which is a year-round intensive training in one sport conducted from an early age because parents want their children to become successful in the world of sports and believe that early commitment is required to achieve this (Côté & Vierimaa, 2014). At the same time, this increase in sport specialization goes hand in hand with a growing concern about burnout among athletes, which is a syndrome characterized by emotional exhaustion caused by becoming less valuable and important (Raedeke & Smith, 2001).

High rates of burnout in young athletes are dangerous from the public health perspective since the researchers indicate that the rate of burnout among athletes varies from 10% to 40% depending on the type of sport and the age group (Gould et al., 1996). There is a relationship between specialization and burnout that should be studied because while early specialization may lead young athletes to stressful conditions, overtraining, and various psychological difficulties that can prevent enjoyment of sports.

The review of literature shows that there are competing theories in the field: models promoting specialization and models promoting multiple sports participation (Baker et al., 2003). On the one hand, the theory of specialization is proved to be successful, but on the other hand, it can lead to psychological problems related to the risk of burnout among young athletes (Ericsson et al., 1993; Stryer et al., 2000).

The purpose of this literature review is to analyze the existing knowledge concerning the relationship between specialization in youth sports and burnout. The review will include empirical findings, different theories, and situational factors that influence the relationship between specialization and burnout in young athletes and will help to understand if specialization is one of the reasons for young athletes’ burnout.

# Training Guide to the Century in just 16 Weeks

## Weeks 1-4: Building the Base
Cyclists should start with 3-4 weekly rides that focus on easy, conversational pace bike rides. By the end of week four of this training, the rider should manage to cover distances of 40-50 miles in their longest ride. The rider should schedule one hill workout per week to get strong but be sure to focus on maintaining consistency throughout this base phase rather than on the intensity of the bike rides.
 
## Weeks 5-8: Making Improvements in Endurance
Increase the number of rides to 4-5 per week, with the longest of them extending to the distance of 60-75 miles. Also, schedule a tempo ride and a hill repeat workout during this phase. In addition, the rider should practice a fueling strategy during the longer rides and test the effectiveness of various gels, drinks, and food options while riding.

## Weeks 9-12: Peak Phase
The rider should maintain 4-5 rides weekly, with the longest ride being 80-90 miles long. The focus at this stage should be to include workouts that involve intervals used in workouts designed to train power and speed and practice rising longer hills while riding at the race pace. The cyclist should also start riding the terrain that they will face during the race and apply their nutrition plan while riding.

## Weeks 13-15: Taper and Mental Preparation
The distance of rides at this stage should decrease by about 30-50% of the distance travelled during the previous weeks. The distance of the longest ride should remain 50-60 miles. Make sure to rest sufficiently, take proper sleep, stretch, and take massages. Check the plan for pacing.

## Week 16: Race
Ride 20-30 miles before the race day and stop riding in 2-3 days before the race properly. Make sure that the gear is working and prepare the final check of all substances and other things which are carried during the race.

# 10 Tips for Successful Succulents on Sunny Windowsills

We can all agree that having succulents in a sunny windowsill is a real paradise for the adorably green cuties. But, this doesn’t mean you can just dump them there and never look back. Here is how to maintain the prosperity of the sun-loving plants.

**1. Choose the Best Species**
By no means all succulents can adapt to sunlight. Echeveria, jade, or aloe prove to be the most successful plants under bright light. Thus, it is better to stick to sun lovers to plant in the sunniest place.

**2. Keep an Eye on Sunburn**
This is a real issue. If you see that your succulent starts being pale and losing its color, the plant needs to move a little bit back into the shade. The solution to the problem is simple: you can use a thin curtain as a filter.

**3. Turn the Pot at Least Once Every Two Weeks**
It is necessary to turn pots once in a week or two weeks to enable even growth of different parts of succulents instead of their stretching towards the necessary source of light.

**4. Avoid Excessive Watering**
This is the main rule. Sunny windows tend to dry out quickly, but succulents like the soil of moderate humidity. Water every 2-3 weeks maximum.

**5. Use Appropriate Substrate**
Get special cactus or succulent substrates. Regular potting soils hardly drain enough moisture.

**6. Ensure Drainage of the Pot**
It is a must that there is a hole in the bottom of the pot. It is worth noting that stagnant water has the potential to kill the whole plant.

**7. Be Careful Of Heat**
Sunny windowsills may be too hot for the plants, and during summer it may become too hot for plants. Air circulation helps a lot.

**8. Fertilize Slightly**
During the growing season, apply diluted fertilizer once a month.

**9. Check For Pests**
Check for the presence of pests such as spider mites or mealy bugs, which threaten succulents while growing in the sun.

**10. Accept the Variety of Growth of Succulents**
It is crucial to let succulents grow naturally. Some plants will be stretched, while others will maintain their compact form.

# Autoplay Characteristics and Planned Media Behaviors

The advent of autoplay has come to question the concept of planned media experiences. By automatically rolling on to the next episode, video or song instead of requiring the user to make the choice, autoplay makes it easier for consumers to consume media passively.

The requirement of having to choose means the addition of a choice, allowing the consumer to reflect on whether they want to continue watching. Autoplay does away with that thought. The only question posed is: do I want to watch another episode? One simply needs to stop the autoplay from continuing.

The autoplay system shows how default settings work. It doesn’t matter whether you want something: if the option is default, it will be used.

Autoplay also exploits psychological vulnerabilities. The mere act of watching leads to an increased appeal of the content referred to as the mere exposure effect. Moreover, beginning with a new activity has much less psychological cost when it is accomplished by the autoplay.

However, autoplay functionality is not always a problem. It makes things easier when there is no need for concentration, e.g. while listening to music or driving. This is when problems arise: autoplay during activities that require concentration.

So, the difference in context changes how disruptive autoplay features are. For example, there is a difference between an instrumental music and some storyline-oriented show, where it is easy to get lost in time. The problem could be conquered by providing either an option of turning autoplay off or making sure the user confirms the action.

To sum up, autoplay does hurt planned behaviors when it comes to media consumption.

#Hybrid Learning Changes the University Lecture Hall

This means that it is impossible to say whether the necessity of going to lectures still exists.

Despite increasing awareness of the importance of transit in sustainable suburban development, there are still many things not known, namely what funding methods work best for transit in different types of suburbs.
