# Inbox Overload: A Modern Workplace Problem

Inbox overload has become a ubiquitous workplace complaint due to several converging factors in our digital era. First, email's accessibility and low barrier to entry mean anyone can send messages to anyone, often without careful consideration. This has normalized excessive communication where copying multiple recipients and sending non-urgent items has become standard practice.

The always-on culture amplifies this problem. With smartphones and notifications, employees feel compelled to check emails constantly, blurring work-life boundaries. Messages that might have been consolidated into one daily briefing now arrive throughout the day and evening, fragmenting attention.

Companies often struggle with communication because they don't have a clear plan for how to talk to each other. This means people end up using email for everything, even when it's not the best way to communicate. For example, simple questions or complicated discussions that would be better suited for a meeting or instant messaging get lost in a crowded inbox. This can lead to unnecessary repetition and distractions, making it harder for people to focus on what's really important.

Additionally, the volume of automated emails has exploded. System notifications, newsletters, promotional content, and automated alerts flood inboxes, making it difficult to identify genuinely important messages.

The absence of effective email management culture exacerbates these issues. Unlike previous generations who developed filing and prioritization systems, many workers lack strategies for managing large volumes. Meanwhile, features like "reply all" and group emails can create endless chain conversations.

Finally, the expectation of rapid email response creates anxiety. Workers feel obligated to maintain inbox zero or respond quickly, treating email as an urgent communication tool rather than an asynchronous one.

Addressing inbox overload requires organizational changes: clearer communication guidelines, designated channels for different message types, automated filtering, and cultural shifts toward respecting attention and reducing unnecessary copying and notifications.

# Charging Into the Future: How Older Neighborhoods Are Adapting to Electric Vehicles

Unlike newer suburban developments built with modern infrastructure, many established urban and suburban communities lack the electrical capacity and dedicated parking spaces needed to support widespread EV charging. Residents in these neighborhoods often rely on street parking and aging electrical grids that weren't designed for the increased demand.

"We're seeing a real infrastructure gap," says Maria Chen, director of urban planning at the Clean Energy Institute. " Homeowners without driveways can't easily install private chargers, and many cities haven't yet deployed sufficient public charging stations."

As EV adoption continues growing, supporting all neighborhoods in this transition will be crucial for achieving climate goals while ensuring no community is left behind in the clean energy revolution.

# The Limits of Facial Recognition Regulation

There are several problems with regulating facial recognition technology too strictly. Firstly, regulations are very location-specific. For instance, strict regulations on facial recognition in one country could have the unintended consequence of advancing the technology in other countries with less regulation. Secondly, too strict regulation might hinder facial recognition innovation in general. In many cases, the costs to comply with regulations are a greater burden to smaller companies, while larger, established companies are better able to cope. Thirdly, regulation does not actually stop criminals or rogue dictators, who will continue to circumvent such rules. And finally, because the technology is changing rapidly, it is hard to keep up with regulations, leading to legal uncertainty. These issues suggest that the blanket regulations that have been proposed by some lawmakers may not be the best course of action.

Facial recognition is already being used in many beneficial contexts, from missing children to airport security to fraud detection. It would be very unfortunate if regulators squelched further progress on this technology, given its usefulness in these cases. And the level of risk varies depending on the context (facial recognition in an airport is very different from using it at a store). A one-size-fits-all approach may not be appropriate.

It is better to use the current legal regime, with laws on data privacy and anti-discrimination (and perhaps laws around warrants), to tackle these issues. But regulators might consider more transparent rules on facial recognition technology, in which companies would have to disclose how well it works with different demographic groups, their error rates, and their policies. Self-regulation of technology with a few legal remedies to address harms is a good approach.

Youth Sports Specialization and Childhood Burnout: A Literature Review

Over the past two decades, there has been an increase in the popularity of sports specialization in the early years of youth athletics. Many factors influence specialization in youth sports including but not limited to the drive and aspiration of parents and children for athletic success, the belief that specialization in one sport is necessary to achieve elite-level performance, and societal expectation (Côté & Vierimaa, 2014). The consequences of specialization in youth sports have generated debate and controversy. Some advocate the benefits of early sports specialization, arguing that it is required to develop elite athletes. However, others advocate a multi-sports model for athlete development arguing that such programs are more holistic, fostering positive psychological development and promoting a healthy lifelong attitude towards physical activity (Baker et al., 2003). Although research has supported links between specialization and elite athletic success, the importance of deliberate practice in the early years, and the value of early sport-specific training, recent evidence has provided an alarming trend in burnout and sport attrition associated with sports specialization in children.

Athlete burnout is a syndrome described by emotional and physical exhaustion, a decrease in feeling of personal accomplishment, and a devaluation of one’s sport (Raedeke & Smith, 2001). Burnout prevalence among youth athletes ranges from 10% to 40% depending on the sport and age groups studied (Gould et al., 1996). Sports specialization is associated with chronic stress and overtraining that may lead to increased risk of burnout. Such psychological stressors can undermine sport enjoyment and long-term participation in sport. This literature review will explore the research linking sports specialization and burnout to evaluate the validity of sports specialization as a risk factor for burnout among youth.

As I walked around the neighborhood where I grew up, I would learn that a lack of public transportation or green space could have disproportionately negative effects on my lower-income neighbors. These observations inspired me to further educate myself on topics like sustainable cities, transit-oriented development, and affordable housing policy. I became interested in how urban planning decisions can have real impacts on how communities function and the everyday lives and economic prospects of their residents.

My passion to contribute to the field of urban planning led me to volunteer on a project with our local planning commission. Working on a community engagement component of a mixed-use development project, I learned how effective planning relies on both technical knowhow and community input. This experience has confirmed for me that strategic changes, such as a well-designed green infrastructure system, mandated affordable housing within a development, or new bike/pedestrian paths, can make a difference in the communities where we live.

In a world that is becoming increasingly urbanized, and experiencing an influx of migration to cities, we must find sustainable and equitable ways of accommodating more people. Urban planning is an interdisciplinary field that uses knowledge and ideas from the social and environmental sciences, quantitative analysis, and design to create more equitable and livable communities, resilient to both climate change and the challenge of housing affordability. A master's degree in planning would offer formal training in planning theory and methodology that would prepare me to implement these practices. I am particularly interested in studying quantitative techniques, and learning practical tools I could apply in my community.

# 16-Week Century Training Guide
## Weeks 1-4: Base Building
- Focus on building consistency and establishing a routine. Ride 3-4 times per week including one longer ride per week that builds up to 40-50 miles in the 4th week. Work on conversational pace and only do one hill workout per week to build fitness. Stay injury free!
## Weeks 5-8: Endurance Development
- Continue the same weekly routine and increase mileage. Include some tempo rides, build up your long ride to 60-75 miles, and continue weekly interval workouts. At this point you should start experimenting with nutrition on long rides to see what works best for you. You should be riding 4-5 times per week by this time.
## Weeks 9-12: Peak Building
- Add some interval workouts to your weekly rides, start tackling some long climbs and get in some race pace work. Keep riding 4-5 times per week and your long ride should be 80-90 miles at this point. If you can mimic the terrain of your century ride, you can prepare more accurately for your day-of ride.
## Weeks 13-15: Taper and Mental Preparation
- Reduce the volume of your rides by about 30-40% and make sure your long ride does not exceed 50-60 miles. You can still do intense rides, but the goal is to get your body to feel fresh and strong. Start making sure you get proper sleep, stretch, get a massage, and rest. Visualize your race day, make sure your nutrition and fueling plan is solid, know the route, have your support packs prepped, and your bike is all checked and ready.
## Week 16: Race Week
- Only do some short 20-30 mile rides and take at least 2-3 full days of rest before your century ride.
- Relax, have fun, and enjoy all the hard work you have put in to get here. Start that ride easy and finish strong!
General Tips
- Make sure that you have at least one day off per week, if your body and life needs more days off then take them
- Make sure you do not increase mileage by more than 10% per week and follow the plan for each week of riding

Succulents do very well placed on windowsills because they love the sunshine. Here are a few pointers to make sure they survive your sunny windowsill:
**4. Not all Succulents Need Equal Amounts of Sun**
Certain types, like Echeveria, jade plants and aloe, thrive in intense bright light. Other types will become pale, or bleached, under too much direct sun. These plants are essentially becoming sunburned. If that happens, place a sheer curtain between them and the sunlight.
**5. Use Well-Draining Soil**
Too much water is a common culprit of poor succulent health. Water your succulents as infrequently as you can, ideally only once every 2-3 weeks. Make sure you are using a cactus or succulent mix in their potting soil rather than potting soil which holds more moisture.
**6. Check Your Pot's Drainage**
Make sure your pot has a drainage hole to allow extra water to drain out. Standing water will harm your succulents.
**7. Provide Air Circulation**
Windowsills can become quite warm and sunny during the summer months, which can stress out succulents. Good air circulation can help prevent this stress.
**8. Rotate Your Succulents**
Succulents will often try to stretch toward the light. You can prevent this by rotating pots every week or two, otherwise your plant may grow lopsided and look like a contortionist.
**9. Fertilize Sparingly & Watch for Pests**
Only fertilize once a month in the summer and spring growing season. Look for pests like spider mites and mealybugs. This is the main time for feeding, just make sure to dilute it first and make sure you are using a fertilizer made for succulents.
**10. Embrace Their Natural Growth**
Sometimes, succulents will stretch and become elongated and sometimes the growth is different and unique. Embrace these natural qualities in your plants and enjoy the changes as they happen.

# Autoplay Features and Intentional Media Habits

Autoplay removes the pause in between media where you ask "do I want to watch another episode?" The absence of an interstitial moment of choice and consciousness, as well as the mere exposure effect, which makes media more enjoyable with increased exposure, leads people to watch longer than they otherwise would have. Autoplay exploits people's natural tendency towards inertia and cognitive bias.
A related phenomenon is "binge drift" and the desire to get through more content.
The flip-side of Autoplay is the "default effect," which refers to people's tendency to adopt default settings for certain options when making choices. Research on default effects has shown that the status quo option is much more likely to be chosen regardless of the option's desirability. Autoplay reverses this bias, making it incumbent on users to opt-out of autoplay.
Autoplay may be a helpful convenience in some contexts (passively listening to music, listening to a new album, listening to a podcast on the train), but in others (e.g., shows and movies requiring sustained attention) it leads to negative consequences. A better option may include contextual default settings for autoplay (i.e., an explicit toggle for users indicating whether the media content should autoplay or not) or autoplay prompts after each episode/movie. In any case, this burden of action should not be on the user to turn off the autoplay feature.

# Hybrid Learning Reshapes the University Lecture Hall

While the term may have originated during pandemic, a hybrid approach to learning isn’t going anywhere.
With a mix of in-person learning and digital resources including recordings and asynchonous assignments, hybrid learning is reshaping the experience of a university lecture. For many, a hybrid lecture is the perfect compromise for both educators and students alike. For others, the shift toward online learning has raised the question of whether in-person attendance is even worth it.
"We're seeing a transformation in how educators approach the large lecture hall," said Dr. Sarah Chen, an educational technology researcher. "It's no longer just about delivering information. It's about creating engagement whether students are physically present or joining remotely."
The option to record lectures for later has been popular with students for its flexibility. Those recordings can be viewed at the learner’s pace, making it easier for international students in different time zones to participate in classes. This has prompted discussions within the university setting regarding whether attendance should still be a requirement for academic success.
There are those who feel that in-person education can never be fully replaced. Professor James Mitchell expressed skepticism about the value of a remote lecture compared to one in-person. "There's a risk of creating a two-tier system where remote students receive diminished educational experiences," Mitchell said. He said that the irreplaceable value of a university education lies in the community experience and opportunities for spontaneous interaction.
The move toward hybrid learning was accelerated during the pandemic, but many educators said it’s sticking around because of its benefits. Universities struggling with budgets in the post-pandemic world are still looking for ways to make education more efficient.
As the discussion continues, leaders in higher education are finding a middle ground. Many universities are now making in-person attendance mandatory for smaller seminars and lab settings, where community building is key, and are using a hybrid model for most other classes.

The incentives facing newsletter writers are much different from traditional media: readers choose to allow these newsletter writers access to their inboxes. This grants the writer a high degree of control and intimacy with the audience, which does not exist in traditional media. This is why it is so easy for bad actors in the traditional media to get away with publishing irresponsible, exaggerated stories.

These newsletter writers are directly accountable to their readers: they are able to get immediate, often personal, feedback when they get something wrong.

The incentive structures are also better in this model: rather than worrying about ad impressions, newsletter writers are financially supported by subscribers. This means that these writers are incentivized to build and keep their audience’s trust, rather than trying to drum up engagement and clickbait for short periods of time.

The main challenge for the newsletters is that there is no gatekeeper. This is the part of the media that used to work, but is now falling short. Without these gatekeepers, bad faith actors can more easily enter the field and spread misinformation; it is too easy for charlatans to make assertions they have no support for, without accountability.

But these challenges have not stopped many from giving up the clickbait that is too often the focus of mainstream media. Many feel that they lack credibility and trustworthiness, especially in the face of corporate control. The newsletter writers are free from these problems, and free to write nuanced, in depth pieces about the things that they are truly experts in, instead of worrying about fitting into a daily news cycle. The move to newsletters is not the irrational choice of some people who are tired of the daily news, it is a perfectly reasonable alternative.

# Public Transit Funding in Growing Suburbs: A Literature Review

Transportation systems face new challenges due to increased urbanization and suburbanization in metropolitan areas. Suburban public transit systems differ from urban systems as they often face distinct issues including lower population density, dispersed development, and greater historical reliance on personal cars. While people are increasingly living in the suburbs, they have historically received less funding for transit. As these areas continue to grow in population, there is an increasing need for effective and reliable public transportation that is accessible to all.

Traditional sources of public transit funding (farebox revenue, local taxation, and state grants) can be insufficient to cover operating costs especially in regions with low-density and low ridership. Consequently, a vast body of literature examines the effectiveness of alternative funding options (public-private partnerships, congestion pricing, developer exaction, etc.) for public transit in suburban areas.

As climate change becomes a priority and work-from-home policies reduce commuting demand in cities, conversations surrounding public transit funding have resurfaced. While there is an abundance of information surrounding the topic, there are many gaps in knowledge. There is no clear consensus as to the most effective public transit funding solutions and some researchers argue that there should be a more regionally-based approach to funding while others argue for more locally-tailored solutions. A literature review was conducted to explore these issues and better understand current gaps in the research.

This literature review will examine public transit funding strategies in the context of growing suburban areas. It will provide an overview of current policy and recent events that have brought public transit funding back into the public eye. Additionally, it will highlight several of the challenges that can hinder the effective implementation of public transit funding, and summarize the existing debates amongst scholars and professionals in the field. In doing so, this literature review aims to shed light on some of the gaps in the existing body of knowledge that need to be addressed, and suggest directions for further research.

# Personal Statement: Environmental Economics
In my childhood, I remember how the pollution issue in our community caused many problems including the poor quality of water and many health issues for people. We knew what the problems were, and we had potential ways to fix them, but action was slow. We soon realized that the problem wasn’t a lack of knowledge or technology, rather, conflicting incentives were causing the problems, and that our policy framework has never adequately accounted for external environmental costs. This experience sparked my interest in understanding the role economics plays in environmental problems and in developing solutions that account for the impacts of our actions on the environment.
I became fascinated by economic instruments to solve these environmental problems. Through my academic exploration of environmental economics and related issues, I have delved into carbon pricing, natural resource management, and biodiversity valuation. Environmental economics uses tools like cost-benefit analysis, market-based solutions, and game theory to analyze problems like how emissions trading schemes work or how to properly assign the cost of resource extraction. In addition to the core economics, the study requires a breadth of understanding of many fields, ranging from economic theory, to the ecology of ecosystems, to policy and decision-making, to human psychology and behavior. By developing economic models and empirical evidence, economists find potential ways to create economic incentives for reducing pollution, protecting resources, and promoting sustainable development.
I want to continue developing my interest in the economics of environmental issues because economic tools hold great promise to provide long-term solutions to some of our greatest societal challenges. We can make great strides by working towards protecting a forest or an endangered species, but by understanding and redesigning economic systems and changing the incentives built into our economy, we can effect larger and more lasting changes.
During my previous studies, I have honed my quantitative skills and analytical abilities to develop my expertise on this subject matter, and I am eager to develop my skills and apply them to real-world problems in the environmental space. Ultimately, I hope to contribute in research and policy development to create markets and economic policies that properly align incentives for environmental conservation, that value the natural world and promote ecological integrity, and that do not sacrifice social equity. I am committed to using strong quantitative and economic skills to advance the goals of sustainable development, and through rigorous and interdisciplinary research, I hope to learn innovative solutions that address economic development and the environment together.

Starting and Maintaining a Neighborhood Book Club
Reach out to neighbors who you think would enjoy a book club via flyers, emails or in-person conversations. Gather interested neighbors to create a neighborhood book club of 6-12 members.
- Set up a regular schedule (i.e. monthly or biweekly) and meeting place (i.e. coffee shop, library, neighborhood member's home) for your book club.
- Take turns hosting meetings.
- Vote on what to read. Have members vote on titles suggested by book club members to determine the month's selection. Choose a variety of genres with approximately 200-300 page lengths to keep the book club interesting and exciting.
- Allow 4-6 weeks for reading the book before the next meeting so that everyone can get through it.
- Share bites and chit chat before beginning your discussion. Once the conversation begins, focus on the book for 60-90 minutes. Have a designated leader for each discussion who starts by asking for initial reactions and then moves the conversation into deeper discussions about themes, characters and writing style. Be mindful of allowing the quieter members a chance to share their viewpoints.
- Address non-participation and commitment to the neighborhood book club early on. Have a conversation with members who do not show up frequently.
- Take your disagreements on what to read as an opportunity for growth. Explore a variety of books and ideas with your neighbors to create a well rounded book club experience.
- Find out if members are still enjoying the neighborhood book club. If the group discussion has lost its bite, survey your group for better ideas on future titles.
- Use social media such as Goodreads to create a reading list and discuss books online.
- Invite authors and librarians from your community to your club.
- Host a neighborhood pot luck with food or clothing inspired by your current book.
- Host a video call with an author.
- Celebrate the book club's anniversary and accomplishments.
Ultimately, your neighborhood book club will become about more than just books, it will be about the friendships that are formed and strengthened in the group discussion.

Avoid being overwhelmed!
Buying a good, usable telescope for between $100-300 is a very doable task. Here are my top tips for making it happen...
1) Don't fall for the hype. Magnification power is one that is commonly over-valued in a new scope. A high-powered scope can produce poor quality views if the aperture is small. Aperture is the key, and should be at least 4 inches (a 6'' reflector would be impressive, without needing a large investment in eyepieces).
2) Refractors and dobsonians are very straight-forward and forgiving types. I would suggest starting with one of these over a more complex mount, especially if you're a beginner.
3) Avoid shaky stands. It is difficult to get a good look at anything through a shaking scope. This can ruin even a really good scope.
4) The ideal scope for any particular person is one that they use, instead of one that is left in the closet. So make sure that it's not so heavy that you won't want to lug it outside to use it.
5) Read some reviews (either here on YouTube or in astronomy forums) on any model you're considering before making the purchase. Often there are issues with certain models that don't show up until after people use the scope for a while.
6) Ask the folks at your local astronomy club, if there is one in your area. Chances are they will let you use their scopes, offer candid advice, and might even let you loan a scope before you invest your hard-earned dollars.
7) Don't skimp on the eyepieces. Quality eyepieces can improve your viewing. That said, I wouldn't recommend spending too much on eyepieces to go with an entry level scope, but beware of bad stock eyepieces that can come with some models.
8) Check out how quickly you can get it setup, and how hard it is to aim the thing, if you want to spend a few hours on a stargazing night outside figuring out what you're doing.

The ethical implications of using AI to generate illustrations in children's picture books are far-reaching, particularly given their formative influence on shaping young readers' perceptions of beauty and diversity. The question of whether such illustrations should be labelled becomes critical in this context.

AI-generated images can perpetuate biases present in the data they are trained on. Children's books play a crucial role in shaping children's understanding of diversity, inclusion, and representation, with illustrations directly influencing the way they perceive gender, race, ability, and other aspects of diversity.

While AI-generated images may perpetuate historical biases regarding race, gender, and ability representation, the process of creating AI-generated art raises important questions about the cultural value of human-created art and the relationship between artists and young readers.

The creation of AI-generated art is done using data from existing art pieces and does not pay artists. Therefore, its use has the potential to further disadvantage illustrators as a profession. In exchange for this, however, AI illustrations offer a reduced cost to produce books.

This offers an opportunity for independent authors or smaller publishers who may not have the resources to hire professional illustrators. However, this should not come at the cost of fair compensation to artists.

This could be through a hybrid model that uses AI and human illustrators together, or through implementing systems that fairly compensate artists.

The use of AI-generated illustrations in children's picture books is not inherently unethical as long as it is done in a way that is responsible and respectful to artists, and beneficial for the representation of children.

More consumers are realizing that they can save a few dollars by having their devices fixed.
Repairing electronic devices can save consumers money and decrease electronic waste.
As a result, a growing right-to-repair movement is attempting to give people more options in fixing their devices.
Electronic waste, also known as e-waste, is one of the fastest-growing waste streams in the world. The toxic materials, including lead and mercury, are harmful to humans and the environment.
But people dispose of around 50 pounds of e-waste per person per year, a fraction of which can be avoided by refurbishing electronic devices.
Repair shops are also popping up in cities around the world, providing cheaper alternatives to manufacturer-owned repair centers.
Companies like iFixit also make a profit by selling repair manuals and parts. The rise of certified refurbished items has also exploded in recent years, offering reliable devices at lower prices.
"People shouldn't have to buy a new phone because the battery dies or the screen cracks," said one repair advocate.
Planned obsolescence and the disposable tech culture that has followed has become a growing concern for many consumers, but many tech manufacturers have resisted calls to make it easier for consumers and independent repair shops to repair devices.
The high costs of repairs and the need to keep devices in order for safety reasons are just a few of the reasons manufacturers have provided for not allowing devices to be serviced by unauthorized workers.
However, recent legislation, such as New York’s Digital Right to Repair Act, or the European Union’s mandate requiring manufacturers to provide repair parts for some electronic goods, has pushed some manufacturers to consider the benefits of right-to-repair laws.
Apple has offered a limited self-repair program that some consumers have described as not going far enough.
The rise of repair advocates, who are often environmentally-conscious, have been pushing back against the notion of throwaway culture and the idea that consumers should be able to fix their devices.
According to analysts, the market is expected to grow in the coming years, as more consumers seek to extend the life of their smartphones, laptops and other appliances that have minor issues that could easily be fixed.

# The Hidden Costs of Rent Stabilization

Rent stabilization limits the prices at which landlords can rent their units. These limits are meant to protect tenants, but they have a range of consequences:
- Reduced incentives for new rental homes to be built and existing ones to be improved.
- Artificially high market rates for tenants in unstabilized housing. (In cities with large numbers of rent stabilized homes, like San Francisco and New York, overall rents in the open market are also extremely high.)
- Ineffective targeting of assistance to lower income people. Rent stabilized units become a valuable prize for tenants to defend, and new residents face insurmountable odds of being priced out of the market, particularly those who are younger and lower income.
- Reduced labor mobility as tenants fear to leave their rent stabilized units.
- Reduced maintenance and disinvestment in rent stabilized homes, which can lower the overall neighborhood standards, and in extreme cases landlords will sell or even abandon homes where costs outstrip their ability to collect rent sufficient to maintain the unit.
The logic of stabilizing rents is to provide an affordable housing option for vulnerable populations. Renters can save on housing costs and invest their money elsewhere, while landlords enjoy steady tenants. However, it is clear that stabilizing rents leads to housing instability. Rather than addressing the underlying causes of unaffordable housing, stabilization treats the symptoms with a price control.

Alternative solutions should target the most vulnerable households with renter assistance. This approach directly targets individuals in need and does not skew market prices. Stabilization should not be considered a viable solution to the affordability crisis, as the result is a smaller number of worse rental units available at higher market rates, all to subsidize privileged tenants with below-market rates. Instead of limiting the ability of landlords and developers to profit from housing development and improvement, we should focus on removing barriers to construction and increasing supply by reforming zoning regulations, reducing the cost of building new homes, and expediting the development process. These reforms will target the housing shortage at the root and increase availability without creating false scarcity.

# Literature Review: Community-Supported Fisheries

With an increased awareness of where food comes from and the processes behind its production, many have started to question the sustainability of their diets. One way in which they are doing so is with community-supported agriculture (CSA) programs. The concept of community-supported agriculture has recently been applied to the marine and freshwater settings as well, through community-supported fisheries (CSF). Through CSFs, consumers commit themselves to the harvest of a local fisher for a price and, in return, receive shares of the catch. CSFs, similar to CSAs, provide a way for both consumers and producers to invest themselves in the local food supply. Instead of being involved in traditional seafood supply chains, they make a personal connection and risk. Though CSFs offer an alternative to the traditional seafood supply chain and offer an opportunity to support small-scale fishers who are challenged by competing with industrial fishing operations, they also face many issues that hinder success. CSFs, like CSA, promote the idea of a sustainable system by educating and incorporating consumers in the process, and lowering a carbon footprint associated with the distribution of seafood. However, issues that include inconsistent supply, difficult logistics, and accepting unfamiliar fish species can challenge the sustainability of CSFs.

There is a large body of literature focused on CSAs, but much less on the relatively new phenomenon of community-supported fisheries. CSF research is also limited to a few main areas: fisheries management, sustainable food systems, and economic development. This literature review intends to look at studies in fisheries science and management, food studies, and community development to provide a sense of what we know about CSFs, and what gaps there are in the literature regarding CSF structures, viability, social impacts, and environmental claims.

Just launched a major project at work? Now’s the time to ask for a promotion.
Follow these steps to make your case:
## Timing Is Everything
Promotions are for performance, not potential. Waiting a couple weeks will ensure everyone recognizes your efforts. Schedule the conversation two to four weeks after launch so stakeholders can review project outcomes.
But don’t catch your manager on a hectic day or when the building is on fire (literally or figuratively). If your manager is visibly stressed, wait.
Before the meeting, set up a formal appointment so your manager isn’t blindsided. Email a calendar invite for 30 minutes and add context like, “I’d like to discuss my career growth and next steps. Do you have 30 minutes this week?”
## Build Your Case
Remember to bring receipts to the negotiation. The most persuasive promotion cases feature strong, quantifiable accomplishments that clearly demonstrate your value to the company and team, such as the revenue you generated or cost savings.
- “Led implementation that increased efficiency by 35%.”
Other proof points may include leadership examples or problem-solving moments where you went the extra mile. Consider improvements to budgets or project timelines and any special recognition you received.
## Present Your Value Proposition
After complimenting your manager and the team for a successful project, ask for your promotion. Stay upbeat and positive while you explain how the project pushed you beyond your job description, expanded your skillset, and demonstrates your capabilities for your next role. For example, “I’ve loved contributing to this team, and I’m proud of what we accomplished. I believe I’m ready for increased responsibility and would like to discuss a promotion to [specific role].”
If your manager hesitates, ask, “What would I need to demonstrate to earn this promotion?”
If your manager refuses, ask, “When can we discuss this again?” Then, clarify the expectations so you leave with a specific date to reconvene and steps you should take to land that promotion.
Follow up with an email to your manager thanking him for the conversation and documenting your next steps.

You don’t necessarily have to spend a ton of money to get concert venue quality sound in your living room. Here’s how:
1. Stop placing your speakers in the corner
Corners and walls can amplify certain frequencies, especially bass frequencies. If you can, place them in the center of the room for the best sound quality.
2. Cut the echo
You can cut echo and reflections by adding soft, sound-absorbing materials such as blankets, carpets, rugs and drapes.
3. Rearrange the furniture
Sometimes all it takes to improve your sound is a quick rearranging of the furniture. Believe it or not, rearranging the furniture and adding soft materials can make a better difference than buying expensive equipment.
4. Upgrade your cables
Bad audio cables can make your sound quality suffer, as they can introduce interference. Decent quality cables that just work as they’re supposed to are still pretty cheap.
5. Get a better source
Lossless audio, or a better streaming service can go a long way to getting the best quality out of your system.
6. Dust off your system
Dust may not seem like a big deal, but it can contribute to a lower quality sound.
7. Make acoustic panels
If you want to take it to the next level and make a bigger difference, you can build your own acoustic panels. Wrap rockwool in a breathable fabric, such as burlap, and you have a DIY acoustic panel. It’s cheaper than purchasing them from a store.
8. Buy a Bluetooth speaker
If you want to spend a little money, but don’t want to spend tons on a complicated system, consider a quality Bluetooth speaker. These days, you can get surprisingly high quality sound from them.
9. Get a cheap amp
Amping up your old speakers might give them a new lease on life, and you might be surprised at the improvement a cheap amp makes to them.
10. Shop thrift
Old, vintage speakers can sometimes be found in thrift stores and online (Facebook Marketplace is a great resource for used speakers) at insanely low prices.

# Inbox Overload: A Modern Workplace Problem
Email accessibility: Anyone can send an email at any time, and the low threshold for sending emails means that senders are less likely to stop and think about whether a recipient actually needs the email, or if there's a better channel to use for the message.
Email overcommunication: CC'ing a bunch of people unnecessarily and emailing low-priority information is normalized behavior for many. Group emails and the “reply all” function create long, convoluted chains.
Constant checking: Smartphones and notifications encourage employees to check emails constantly, which blurs the line between work and personal life. Instead of receiving a daily digest, employees’ attention is fragmented with individual emails arriving throughout the day and night.
Lack of clarity around which channels should be used: Absent company guidelines, email becomes the default communication option for situations that would be better suited to instant messaging or even an in-person meeting.
A lack of organization tools: Without filters and effective filing systems, employees’ inboxes become clogged with marketing materials, newsletters, automated notices, alerts, etc.
Cultural issues: Employees may view email as more urgent than it is intended to be (inbox zero, assumptions about quick response time, etc.).
Solutions:
Establish clear protocols around which channels should be used and designate different channels for different needs.
Implement filters and change workplace culture to be more conscious about minimizing CCs and notifications.
Essentially, this is a problem that stems from a number of sources. Overload occurs when employees are over-connected, when email is not the best communication tool, and when employees’ attention is being unnecessarily fragmented.

# The Limits of Facial Recognition Regulation

While facial recognition technology should be appropriately overseen we risk undermining its potential benefits and creating inefficiencies in regulation which ultimately risks undermining public safety and innovation.

Comprehensive regulation operates under the assumption that technology can be controlled through legislation. In reality facial recognition is used across very different legal jurisdictions worldwide. With strict restriction in one area we risk simply moving development elsewhere where oversight may be less rigorous. Rather than safeguarding citizens over regulation creates a compliance burden only large established corporations can meet. Unimpeded by such restrictions we see continued use by criminal gangs and authoritarian regimes.

Second, technology develops quickly so by the time legislation is drawn up to cover current capabilities it will already be outdated. As a result restrictive policies quickly become obsolete requiring frequent updating. This creates uncertainty in the law which risks undermining legitimate innovation in areas where facial recognition could bring real benefit e.g. airport security, finding missing children and tackling fraud.

The privacy concerns underlying much regulatory thinking are legitimate but often overblown. Existing laws already address key issues e.g. data protection, anti-discrimination and the need for a warrant. They effectively govern use of facial recognition without need for specific legislation which risks unnecessarily limiting useful applications.

Context matters. For example risks of using facial recognition at a border checkpoint will be very different to using it in a retail environment. But often we see across the board restrictions which either overly restrict legitimate uses or leave insufficient safeguards where most needed. More effective would be sector specific approaches rather than blanket bans.

More effective than restrictive regulation would be transparency and accountability mechanisms. For example requiring evidence of demographic accuracy, error rate and policy would enable informed oversight without need for blanket restrictions. Combined with targeted legal remedies where there is evidence of harm this would allow genuine issues to be addressed without stifling innovation.

Facial recognition technology could bring significant benefit to society. Through appropriate safeguards its use should be allowed. But heavy handed regulation misses the point. More appropriately existing legal frameworks could be built upon, selective restrictions could be used and transparent use could be ensured.

# Youth Sports Specialization and Childhood Burnout: A Literature Review

Over the past 20 years there has been considerable change in the landscape of youth sports. Increasingly there is focus on early specialization and competitive training (Jayanthi et al., 2015). Defined as intensive year round training in one sport from an early age, specialization of sport has become more common in young athletes. This is partly due to parental aspirations, social pressures and belief that early commitment is essential if they are to pursue elite status (Côté & Vierimaa, 2014).

Along with this there has been growing concern about burnout in young athletes. This is a multidimensional syndrome involving emotional exhaustion, reduced sense of accomplishment and devaluation of sport (Raedeke & Smith, 2001). Burnout in young athletes is an important public health issue. Preliminary evidence suggests up to 40% of young athletes across different sports may experience burnout depending on age and sport (Gould et al., 1996). It seems important to consider whether and how specialization might increase risk of burnout in young athletes. Through chronic stress, overtraining and psychological strain early specialization may reduce enjoyment of sport and long term engagement.

In the existing literature there is tension between models of single sport specialization focusing on deliberate practice and skill development and multi-sport participation which emphasizes more holistic development and intrinsic motivation (Baker et al., 2003). Some studies suggest early specialization supports pathways to elite performance but more recently there has been emerging evidence of possible psychological costs including risk of burnout (Ericsson et al., 1993; Stryer et al., 2000).

In this review the current evidence of the relationship between specialization in youth sports and burnout is considered. Drawing on empirical evidence, theoretical foundations and factors in the context of sport the review explores whether specialization represents an important risk factor for burnout in childhood. Where possible the review identifies mechanisms by which specialization might reduce risk of negative psychological outcomes in young athletes.

# 16-Week Century Training Guide

## Weeks 1–4: Base Building
Start with three or four rides a week at conversational pace. Focus on easy cycling. By week four increase the longest ride to 40-50 miles. Add one hill workout per week to build muscular strength. More important than intensity is consistency of effort. This supports injury prevention.

## Weeks 5–8: Endurance Development
Up to four or five rides per week. Longest ride should be 60-75 miles. Add tempo ride (longer sustained hard effort) and hill repeats into the week. Start experimenting with fueling on longer rides. Try different gels, bars and drinks to find what sits well in the stomach.

## Weeks 9–12: Peak Building
Keep four or five rides per week including one of 80-90 miles. Add interval work into the week to build power and speed. Start climbing longer hills at race pace. Test nutrition plan over whole ride. Try to replicate terrain of the century.

## Weeks 13–15: Taper and Mental Preparation
Reduce mileage by 30-40% per week but keep it at similar intensity. Longest ride should be 50-60 miles. Focus on recovery with sufficient sleep, stretching and massage. Look at pacing plan, aim to keep first half conservative then aim for better output in second half.

## Week 16: Race Week
Keep rides short and easy (20-30 miles). Rest two or three days before the event. Check gear, nutrition and route. Take all support stuff out with you. Do final check of bike.

## General Tips
- allow at least one full rest day per week
- regular nutrition and hydration
- listen to body and consider extra recovery days
- progressive increases in mileage (max 10% per week)
- ride on similar terrain to century route

# 10 Tips for Succulents on Sunny Windowsills

To be blunt: succulents on a sunny windowsill are almost ideal in terms of growing conditions. That said their need for light doesn't mean one can put them on the windowsill and leave them there. Here are some guidelines for keeping succulents in good health in high light.

# 1. Choose the Right Varieties

Not all succulents will thrive in high light. In particular echeveria, jade plants and aloe do well in bright conditions. Where possible sun-tolerant species should be picked for most exposed positions.

# 2. Watch for Sunburn

There is risk of sunscald. Pale or bleached leaves could be a sign they've been getting too much direct sun. Where necessary this could be reduced using a sheer curtain to filter the light.

# 3. Rotate Regularly

Every one to two weeks rotate the pots so they develop evenly and don't lean toward the light. This is fundamental to succulent care.

# 4. Do Not Overwater

Sunny windowsills dry out the soil more quickly but succulents still need fairly dry conditions between waterings. Two or three weeks max.

# 5. Use Well-Draining Soil

A cactus/succulent growing mix should be used. Normal potting soil retains too much moisture and under such conditions succulents struggle. There should be a hole in the base of the pot. Without this there is risk of water sitting at the base damaging roots.

# 6. Ensure Adequate Pot Drainage

In summer windowsills can get quite hot risking heat stress. Good air flow will help moderate this.

# 7. Be Mindful of Heat

Over the growing season (spring and summer) a monthly feed with diluted succulent fertilizer should be enough.

# 8. Fertilize Lightly

Even in good growing conditions succulents should be checked regularly on the windowsill for mealybugs and spider mites.

# 9. Monitor for Pests

Where possible let them develop in line with their own natural tendencies. Some will show etiolation, others won't. This is part of their nature.

# 10. Embrace Natural Growth Patterns

Provided the above guidelines are followed windowsill succulent growing could prove very rewarding.

# Autoplay Features and Intentional Media Habits

Autoplay features sit at odds with intentional media consumption. By automatically moving onto the next episode, video or song they reduce the friction of finishing one piece of content and starting another. As a result passive consumption becomes the most straightforward route.

Whereas with active selection users face a decision point; a chance to consider whether they really do want to continue. With autoplay they bypass this cognitive checkpoint. Instead of asking themselves "do I want to watch another episode?" they now need consciously to break an automatic progression. This flips the default burden with important consequences for behavior. Research of default settings shows whatever option requires least action is disproportionately adopted whatever its relevance to the user. Autoplay therefore risks pushing users toward content they may not actually want but would struggle to justify actively choosing.

Autoplay also plays on well known psychological vulnerabilities. Through continued consumption content becomes more appealing (the mere exposure effect). And as noted in academic research starting new content has lower activation energy if it happens automatically meaning we often end up consuming much more than intended ("binge drift").

That said autoplay isn't always problematic. For example in routine commutes or background music it significantly improves convenience. Where it becomes more of a problem is where it becomes the default for content requiring more sustained deliberation.

Key to this is context. Autoplay of instrumental music sits quite differently to autoplay of narrative programming where users often struggle to keep track of time. To balance user autonomy and convenience platforms could consider adding autoplay toggles by content type or alternatively requiring periodic re-engagement of content.

In essence autoplay features do undermine intentional media habits particularly where we're engaging with more complex media. To reclaim intentionality we need either better design of defaults across platforms or users actively turning off these features. The latter though requires more effort than would be justified by good technological design.

# Hybrid Learning Reshapes the University Lecture Hall

Universities across the globe are moving away from the traditional lecture model and increasingly adopting hybrid learning which blends in-person and remote teaching. This enables more flexible routes of learning for students.

This process was accelerated by the pandemic but continues now as institutions see tangible value in hybrid learning. Rather than moving away from lectures altogether they are thinking about them in more interactive terms supported by digital content, recorded lectures and asynchronous learning materials available to all students wherever they choose to attend.

"More and more we're seeing a move away from lectures as information delivery towards more interactive experiences supported by digital content," says Dr. Sarah Chen, educational technology researcher at Cambridge University. "Whereas once you'd sit in a lecture hall listening to a 90 minute talk you might now spend part of that time listening remotely while engaging in more interactive activities in person. Or engage with digital content before or after attending."

Many institutions now routinely record lectures. This allows students to go back over material at a time convenient for them. Particularly useful for international students this gives them scope to engage with content across time zones. Increasing accessibility has raised questions about whether attendance at lectures should still be compulsory for academic success.

Some argue however that through a hybrid approach we risk reducing the university experience. Certain academics feel spontaneous discussion, interaction between students and staff and building a sense of community on campus cannot easily be delivered through online means.

"Without doubt we risk building up a two tier system where students attending remotely will experience a less rich educational environment," says Professor James Mitchell of Oxford University.

A common theme emerging among university administrators is they want to retain the value of in-person lectures through their social and collaborative element but use technology to build on learning outcomes. Increasingly they're focusing on smaller seminar sessions and laboratory work as activities best suited to in-person delivery. Recorded lectures and online discussions have more of a supporting role.

As universities recover from the pandemic and face budget pressures we think we'll see greater use of hybrid learning with significant savings against traditional lecture delivery without necessarily moving away from traditional academic settings. In future the lecture hall will more often be accessible, more technologically enabled and more flexible than its predecessors. As a result attending university will take on a different meaning.

# The Rise of Newsletter Writers as Trusted Commentators

In an age of waning trust in institutions we increasingly see newsletter writers stepping up as reliable commentators. Unlike other media outlets motivated by clicks and corporate interests many independent newsletter creators have built credibility through accountability and authenticity.

Where often mainstream media fails to build relationship with their audience newsletter writers succeed. Subscribers actively ask these writers into their inbox creating an intimate channel of communication. Through this they are more likely to see when a writer gets something wrong and will call them out. This in turn creates strong incentive for accuracy and honesty. Something increasingly absent from many institutional gatekeepers.

Supporting this credibility is their own economic model. Many successful newsletter writers build their income through subscriptions not advertising. As a result they have no incentive to sensationalize or mislead. Their own interests lie in building long term trust with readers not chasing short term engagement. It's hard to overstate the advantage this gives over more ad supported media.

Many also bring strong expertise of their own chosen topic. As a result they are able to focus on deeper analysis rather than reacting to short term news cycles. Readers value this and increasingly gravitate towards voices that add context and nuance rather than clickbait headlines.

There are risks in the newsletter ecosystem. Without editorial oversight we risk poor research or unsupported claims. And given the low barrier to entry we could see charlatans alongside genuine experts.

But overall the trend is clear. More and more readers trust independent newsletter writers precisely because they've ditched the institutional structures underpinning traditional journalism. As increasingly in mainstream media engagement is prioritized over truth we see this credibility gap being filled by newsletter writers. Their rise is more a reflection of a real market failure in mainstream media than any flaw in information consumption. And more importantly it sits on audiences making considered decisions about who they trust.

# Public Transit Funding in Growing Suburbs: A Literature Review

Rapid suburbanization of metropolitan areas across North America and around the globe has presented significant challenges for developing and maintaining transit infrastructure. As populations move out into the suburbs demand for reliable and accessible public transport has increased. However funding mechanisms have struggled to keep pace with demand.

Public transit in the suburbs is very different from in the city. Typically we see lower population densities, more spread out development and historically stronger preference for private car use when commuting. As a result we have seen much less investment in transit in the suburbs relative to their growing population. This has raised distinct challenges in funding suburban transit systems compared with more traditional urban transit. Often traditional revenue sources (e.g. farebox revenue, local taxes and state grants) simply do not cover costs of serving lower density areas with more limited ridership.

In recent years a range of more diversified funding options have been explored in academic work. These include public-private partnerships, developer exactions, congestion pricing and regional funding mechanisms. More recently concerns of climate change and changing commuting patterns (supported by increasing use of remote working) have led to renewed debate about priorities for transit investment.

Taken together the literature shows a range of views on most appropriate funding mechanisms. Some argue through regional coordination and pooling of funding we could more fairly allocate resources between different suburban systems. Others highlight need for local control and local solutions suited to specific suburban contexts. At policy level federal and state frameworks influence the capacity to invest in transit in the suburbs but vary across jurisdictions.

While there is increasing recognition of the role of transit in sustainable development of our suburbs much remains to be learned about which funding mechanisms are most appropriate for different types of suburb. In this review the author considers existing academic work on funding of suburban transit looking at sources of funding, policy innovation and outcomes. The aim is to better understand current challenges of funding suburban transit and identify where there may be useful practice to support future transit development in growing suburban communities.

# Starting and Maintaining a Neighborhood Book Club

## Getting Started

Start by finding interested neighbors through email, flyers or chance conversation. A membership of 6-12 people works well enabling meaningful discussion without becoming too unwieldy logistically.

Set up regular meetings (biweekly or monthly) at a convenient time and location e.g. someone's home, local coffee shop or public library.

## Selecting Books

Use a democratic process for choosing the next read with members putting forward titles and voting on them. Try different genres to keep members engaged. Consider length and complexity. Most groups find novels between 200 and 300 pages work well. Allow at least 4-6 weeks between meetings.

## Structuring Meetings

To build a sense of community include light refreshments at the start of each meeting. Set aside 60-90 minutes for discussion. Start with general reactions before moving into themes, prose style and characterization. Make a conscious effort to involve quieter members.

Each meeting could have a discussion leader to help keep the conversation focused and productive.

## Keeping Momentum

To share the workload rotate who hosts. To broaden members' literary experience include a mix of popular fiction, canonical works and less well known books. Occasionally consider bringing in a local author or librarian as guest speaker.

To avoid people feeling left out set expectations of participation at the start. If someone regularly doesn't attend follow up with them individually.

## Sustaining Interest

To add variety consider themed potlucks, going along to author events or arranging video calls with authors. Use a platform such as Goodreads to keep a running reading list. Recognize key milestones e.g. anniversary of the club.

Often as much as literature members join book clubs for the sense of community. Over time genuine friendships develop as they spend time together outside the formal discussion.

## Handling Challenges

Where there is disagreement about book choice remind members engaging with different views will enrich discussion. If at some point the group feels stale ask members what they'd like to read next and adjust the program accordingly.

# 10 Tips for Choosing a Beginner-Friendly Telescope

If you'd like to dip your toes into exploring the cosmos without stretching your budget here are some pointers to help you choose your first telescope without undue frustration or financial risk. This can't be overstated.

1. Establish your budget first.

At this stage you don't need a top-end instrument. A good beginner telescope will usually cost between $100 and $300.

2. Opt for a refractor or Dobsonian.

This is about right as a starting point. Such instruments are much more user friendly than those with complex mounts. Through intuitive handling they suit the novice observer.

3. Do not fixate on magnification.

You might think high magnification would be good but in reality it's overrated. A 6 inch reflector will give good views without needing too many eyepieces.

4. Prioritize aperture.

Better views will come from a larger objective lens/mirror. If possible aim for minimum 4 inch aperture.

5. Stability is critical.

Significantly the quality of your scope and stability of your tripod will have a big impact on your own observing experience. It's worth investing in a good mount for future usability.

6. Consult user reviews.

On astronomy forums and video sites you'll find honest views from experienced users of different instruments. They don't hide up downsides of a particular product.

7. Evaluate the included eyepieces.

Eyepiece quality affects performance. Often the eyepieces included with entry level instruments aren't up to much.

8. Account for portability.

If you find yourself needing to take your telescope out regularly consider size and weight.

9. Prioritize ease of setup.

An instrument easy to deploy will be more likely to be used regularly than one where setting up is complex.

10. Join a local astronomy club.

Many clubs will let members try different instruments, give honest recommendations and in some cases borrow equipment before deciding whether to buy. Most importantly the best telescope is one you'll use. Choose something which suits your lifestyle and keeps your enthusiasm up.

Happy stargazing!

# The Ethics of AI-Generated Artwork in Children's Books

There are important ethical considerations of using AI generated artwork in children's books which warrant consideration.

# Key arguments for

Key arguments for include efficiency and accessibility. AI could lower the cost of producing illustrated children's books making it more affordable for smaller publishers. And may open up illustration to more independent authors who otherwise wouldn't be able to afford to commission an artist.

# But there are important concerns

But there are important concerns. First one needs to consider compensation for artists and risk of job displacement. Often AI systems are trained on existing artwork without permission or reward for the original creator. Many professional illustrators already live precarious financial lives. They risk losing out in this part of the market which has traditionally valued human creativity.

Second, in children's books illustration has pedagogic value. Through illustrations young readers learn about representation of themselves and others; of beauty and diversity. Through training on existing data AI systems could entrench historic biases about e.g. race, gender and ability.

Third one needs to consider the value and authenticity of the work. Traditionally in children's literature there is recognition of meaningful links between human creators and young readers. With AI generated artwork this link is lost. This risks reducing cultural value of the work.

# Possible ethical routes forward

Possible ethical routes forward could include; clear labeling of illustrations where AI has been used so readers are aware of how their book was created. Publishers could commit to using AI tools to support but not replace human artists. Or where they use existing professional artwork in their training data they could ensure appropriate compensation.

On its own, use of AI artwork in children's books is not unethical. But it does need careful consideration of its application. To fully exploit the efficiency benefits one needs to consider risks of undermining artists' livelihoods, risks of reinforcing bias through illustrations and consider child development. Without these considerations the ease of use of AI could prove too costly.

# Right to Repair Movement Gains Momentum as Consumers Embrace Electronics Refurbishment

As electronic waste builds up in landfills across the globe a growing movement is encouraging consumers to repair and refurbish their own devices rather than bin them. This challenges the culture of disposability which has dominated the technology industry for decades.

At its heart the movement is about consumers' right to service their own smartphone, laptop and appliances without having to rely on expensive services from the manufacturer. Its supporters argue it cuts down electronic waste, saves money and allows people to continue using often perfectly functional devices. "People shouldn't have to buy a new phone because the battery dies or the screen cracks," said one repair advocate.

Across cities around the world independent repair shops have risen offering more affordable alternatives to official service centers. And companies such as iFixit have built up successful businesses selling repair guides and replacement parts.

Environmentally this makes sense. E-waste contains toxic substances such as lead and mercury and is a major source of pollution. Through refurbishment consumers could avoid around 50 pounds of e-waste per person each year according to environmental studies.

In the past manufacturers have resisted the movement saying unauthorized repair risks compromising security and safety of their devices. However legislative moves are starting to change the regulatory landscape. New York introduced the digital right to repair act and the EU ruled manufacturers must provide spare parts for some electronics. Technology firms including Apple have started running limited repair programs but critics say they don't go far enough.

At the same time considerable growth has been seen in the market for refurbished electronics. With established quality standards they can represent significant cost savings compared with buying new.

Industry analysts expect the repair and refurbish market will continue to grow as increasing environmental concerns lead more consumers to question planned obsolescence.

What started as a grassroots movement is now moving into mainstream awareness. It's starting to shift how society thinks about consumption of electronics and waste.

# The Hidden Costs of Rent Stabilization

While rent stabilization programs are well meaning and aim to prevent tenant displacement they create important economic tradeoffs ultimately undermining the housing market and leaving vulnerable groups worse off.

By reducing incentives for property investment and maintenance rent controls suppress supply. Without ability to charge market rent landlords have less incentive to upgrade existing units or build new housing. This creates pressure in uncontrolled markets for prices to rise reducing overall housing affordability. We see this in cities such as New York and San Francisco where in areas with strict rent control average rents are highest. As limited affordable stock becomes more competitive.

Rent stabilization distorts housing allocation. Stabilized units become a scarce commodity creating perverse incentives. Existing tenants benefit disproportionately compared with new applicants often younger and from lower income backgrounds. As a result labor mobility is reduced with workers less likely to move for work where they face difficulty finding affordable housing. In effect the policy ends up favoring already housed people from lower income backgrounds.

Where rental income cannot support improvements property maintenance declines. Landlords cut spending leading to deterioration of individual properties and neighborhoods. In some cases where costs exceed revenue under rent control landlords abandon their property further reducing housing supply.

Only a minority of people will benefit from rent stabilization. A small and fortunate group will see artificially low rents but create negative externalities for all other market participants. Compared with direct assistance programs this is an inefficient mechanism of supporting low income renters. It doesn't address underlying affordability problems but risks distorting the wider housing market.

At its heart price controls seek to treat the symptoms not the causes of affordability. More effective would be increasing housing supply through zoning reform, reducing barriers to construction and improving efficiency of development approvals. In this way we increase availability of affordable housing without creating artificial scarcity.

Rent stabilization is well intentioned but has counterproductive outcomes. Through suppression of supply and misallocation of housing resources it risks undermining those it sets out to help and creating wider economic inefficiency. More effective alternatives focused on expanding supply and targeted assistance would better support housing affordability.

# Literature Review: Community-Supported Fisheries

In response to increasing concern about the sustainability of the food system, community resilience and environmental impact of industrial fishing, there is growing scholarly and practical interest in community supported fisheries (CSF) as one possible route to more environmentally aware and equitable production and distribution of seafood.

Building on the principles of community supported agriculture (CSA), CSF sees consumers buy shares/memberships of local fishing operations in return for regular deliveries of catch. In return they take on financial risk and responsibility for environmental stewardship. Like its agricultural counterpart, CSF sits at the interface between consumer and producer. Rather than through anonymous supply chains, consumers develop direct links with producers and become more aware of where their food comes from. This increases transparency, responsibility and trust between consumer and producer.

In practice, CSF has the potential to address a range of sustainability challenges: reducing carbon footprint of seafood distribution; helping small scale fishers under pressure from competition with industrial fisheries; and through consumer awareness and involvement encouraging more responsible harvest of wild fish.

Compared to its agricultural equivalent, however, CSF is less well researched. Much of the existing literature on CSA explores business models, environmental and social impacts. In contrast, findings from CSF tend to sit across fisheries management, sustainable food systems and economic development literature. This reflects the more recent emergence of CSF as both a practice and focus for academic study. Taken together, existing studies suggest considerable potential but also important challenges including variability of catch, complexity of logistics and building consumer trust of unfamiliar species and supply.

In this review, the current evidence base of community supported fisheries is examined, looking at their underlying structure, claims of environmental sustainability, economic viability and social value. Drawing on scholarship from fisheries science, food systems and community development, key themes, gaps in evidence and opportunities for future research into this developing food system model are identified.

# How to Request a Promotion Following the Completion of a Major Project

## Timing Is Everything

Wait two to four weeks after launching a project. This gives time for the dust to settle and for stakeholders to see results. Don't make your request if there's a crisis or your manager is obviously stressed.

## Build Your Case

Use specific metrics to show your own contribution:
- revenue saved/gained
- team members you developed
- problems you solved yourself
- improved budget/timeline

Where you can quantify it add value e.g. "led implementation" is less strong than "led implementation which improved efficiency by 35%".

## Schedule a Formal Conversation

Don't go straight to your manager. Email them "I'd like to discuss my career development and next steps. Do you have 30 minutes this week?" This gives them time to prepare and shows you're professional.

## Structure the Discussion

Start by showing real pride at the success of the project and your own role in it. Then move on to ask for promotion e.g. "I've enjoyed my role on this team and am proud of what we delivered. I think now I could take on more responsibility so would like to discuss a promotion to [specific role]"

## Present Your Value Proposition

Explain your rationale for wanting promotion e.g.
- good track record of performance
- developed new skills
- showed leadership
- moved well beyond what was expected of me in my existing role

## Listen and Respond

Your manager could say yes, no or that they think timing needs more consideration. If they aren't sure ask them "what would I need to do to be considered for this promotion?" Look for specific actionable feedback.

## Follow Up in Writing

Email up a summary of your conversation and any agreed next steps. That way you have accountability and a record of what was said.

## Handle Rejection Constructively

If they say no ask when you could revisit your request. Ask them what criteria they would use next time and agree to work to meet this.

Promotion is about demonstrated performance. Most of your strongest evidence will be from your own role on this project. Use it well.

# 10 Tips for Improving Home Audio on a Budget

It is entirely possible with a modest budget to achieve concert quality sound in a listening environment. High quality audio reproduction needn't cost a great deal of money. Here are some practical steps to add value to home audio without breaking the bank.

**1. Start with placement.**

Before buying anything consider moving speakers. A central position in the room tends to give the most balanced soundstage. Corners and walls will enhance bass response.

**2. Add soft furnishings.**

Aesthetic benefits of curtains, rugs and blankets are well known but they also have acoustic value. They reduce reverberation and absorb reflected sound. This is an easy low/no cost improvement.

**3. Go wireless.**

Audio quality in bluetooth speakers has improved significantly and they represent much more value for money than high end wired systems. Often the limiting factor is not the speakers themselves but rather a high quality streaming service or use of lossless audio format.

**4. Upgrade your source.**

Often it isn't the speakers that need upgrading but the amplifier. A decent amplifier will add considerable life to old speakers and is readily available cheaply. Good sources include local secondhand shops and on sites such as facebook marketplace.

**5. Invest in a budget amplifier.**

Vintage speakers available at fraction of their original retail price through secondhand channels often have very good acoustic performance. Again they are readily available through local secondhand shops and online.

**6. Hunt for used gems.**

Fabric covered panels using rockwool are easy to make at much less cost than their commercially produced equivalents.

**7. DIY acoustic panels.**

Audio performance will suffer as dust builds up on speakers. Through regular maintenance performance can be reliably improved.

**8. Clean your equipment.**

Very low quality cables can add interference so these should be avoided. There needn't be significant spend on cables but quality should be considered.

**9. Check your cables.**

Often through thoughtful use of soft materials and furniture more can be achieved than expensive equipment upgrades. This should not be underestimated.

**10. Room treatment matters most.**

Underlying all this is that informed selective spending will more often add value than indiscriminate spending. Start modestly, listen critically and consider incremental upgrades and value will be seen for both money and audio.
