# Inbox Overload: A Modern Workplace Problem

Inbox overload is now a common complaint in the workplace. This reflects a range of factors in our increasingly digital age.

First email's ease of use and low entry point means anyone can send anyone else a message. As a result we now see widespread excessive communication with multiple people copied on messages and non urgent items routinely sent by email.

This is compounded by the always on culture. With increasing use of smartphones and push notifications employees feel pressure to regularly check their email. Often this sits on top of existing personal commitments. The boundary between personal and professional time becomes blurred. Messages which previously could easily have formed part of a daily briefing now trickle through during the day and into the evening fragmenting sustained attention.

Often underlying this are communication failings at organizational level. Many companies have no clear guidance on which communication channel should be used for different types of message. As a result individuals default to email for example to ask a quick question or discuss something more complex which would be better suited to a meeting or via instant messaging. As a result we see unnecessary duplication and informational noise.

In addition we now see much more automated email appearing in inboxes e.g. system notifications, newsletters, promotional content and automated alerts. This makes it harder to pick up important messages.

Where there isn't an effective email management culture individuals often lack strategies for dealing with high volumes of messages. Previous generations developed filing systems and prioritization of their mail. Today many workers simply haven't developed similar approaches. Features such as "reply all" and threaded email often lead to lengthy chain conversations.

Finally we increasingly see expectation of quick response to email. Workers feel pressure to keep their inbox at zero or respond quickly. As a result they treat email as more of an urgent than asynchronous form of communication. This creates anxiety in the workplace.

# Charging Into the Future: How Older Neighborhoods Are Adapting to Electric Vehicles

With increasing take-up of electric vehicles across the country we're seeing challenges in older residential neighborhoods keeping pace with the move to green energy.

Unlike more recent developments in the suburbs many established urban and suburban communities simply don't have the electrical capacity or space for private parking to support widespread EV charging. Often residents here will use street parking and their existing (often aging) electrical supply.

"Homeowners without driveways won't easily be able to install their own charger and many cities still haven't rolled out enough public charging," says Maria Chen, director of urban planning at the Clean Energy Institute.

A number of municipalities are responding. Over the next two years Portland, Oregon will roll out 50 public charging stations in under-served neighborhoods. And building owners across New York City are being encouraged to retrofit older apartment complexes to include charging.

In some areas community groups are stepping in. Boston EV Access Initiative works with local groups to look at best location for charging infrastructure and campaigns for fair access across different income groups.

But there remain considerable challenges. Costs of installing a charger can be more than $2,000 and it can be costly to upgrade existing electrical systems. Some residents have raised concerns of the safety and aesthetics of charging infrastructure at street level.

Nevertheless advocates believe it's important we support all neighborhoods in the move to electric vehicles. "These are our most diverse and walkable neighborhoods," says transportation analyst James Rodriguez. "Not only is it environmentally right we need to build charging infrastructure here but it's socially fair."

As more people move to electric vehicles it will be important we support all neighborhoods in this transition if we are to meet our climate ambitions and avoid leaving whole communities behind in the clean energy revolution.

# The Limits of Facial Recognition Regulation

While facial recognition technology needs oversight, restrictive regulation risks limiting genuine benefits and causing inefficiencies in regulation ultimately undermining public safety and innovation.

Comprehensive regulation rests on the assumption technology can be controlled through legislation. But facial recognition exists in different forms across different jurisdictions with very different legal settings. By imposing strict restrictions in one location we simply move development elsewhere where oversight may be less robust. In reality over regulation risks increasing compliance burden only affordable by large existing corporations. Meanwhile criminals and authoritarian regimes face no restrictions.

More importantly regulation struggles to keep up with developing technology. By the time legislation is drafted responding to current capability the technology will have moved on. Restrictive policies rapidly become outdated requiring repeated updating. This creates uncertainty in the law which risks undermining legitimate innovation where facial recognition could bring benefit e.g. airport security, locating missing children and detecting fraud.

Driving regulatory activity are legitimate privacy concerns but they are often overblown. Existing legal frameworks already tackle key issues; warrant requirements, data protection and anti-discrimination. They deliver appropriate safeguards against use of facial recognition without needing specific legislation which could inadvertently restrict beneficial applications.

Often the risks of facial recognition depend on context. At a border checkpoint we face different risks than in a retail store. Yet under general regulation the same rules would apply. As a result we risk either over restrictive limitations of legitimate applications or insufficient safeguards where they are needed. Better value would be delivered through more sector specific approaches than blanket bans.

More effective than restrictive regulation would be mechanisms of transparency and accountability. For example requiring recording of error rate of systems, accuracy across different demographics and their policy of use would support informed oversight without needing restrictive rules. Combined with existing legal remedies for demonstrated harms (eg discrimination) we could use more targeted self-regulation across sectors. This would allow genuine problems to be tackled while enabling innovation where appropriate.

Facial recognition technology offers substantial benefits to society. While safeguards are necessary, heavy-handed regulation misses the mark. Smarter approaches—transparent deployment, selective restrictions, and existing legal frameworks—better balance innovation with legitimate privacy concerns.

# Youth Sports Specialization and Childhood Burnout: A Literature Review

Over the past two decades there has been considerable change in the nature of youth sports. Increasingly there has been emphasis on early competitive training and specialization of talent in one sport (Jayanthi et al., 2015). In response to perceived need for early commitment to attain elite status parents increasingly seek year-round intense training of their children in one sport (Côté & Vierimaa, 2014). As a result more young athletes are pursuing single sport specialization at an early age.

Along with this there has been increasing concern about burnout in young athletes. This is a multidimensional syndrome involving emotional exhaustion, loss of sense of accomplishment and devaluation of sport (Raedeke & Smith, 2001).

Burnout in young athletes is an important public health issue. Preliminary evidence suggests up to 40% of young athletes across different sports and age groups may experience burnout (Gould et al., 1996). It is important to consider whether specialization increases risk of burnout in young athletes. Through chronic stress, overtraining and psychological strain early specialization could reduce enjoyment and longer term engagement of developing athletes.

In the literature there are conflicting models of single sport specialization based on deliberate practice and skill development, and multi-sport participation emphasizing holistic development and intrinsic motivation (Baker et al., 2003). Some studies suggest early specialization supports achievement pathways but more recently there has been evidence of possible psychological costs including risk of burnout (Ericsson et al., 1993; Stryer et al., 2000).

In this review current evidence of the relationship between specialization in youth sports and burnout is considered. Through consideration of theoretical foundations, empirical evidence and contextual factors influencing this relationship the review explores whether specialization represents an important risk factor for burnout in childhood. Where possible the review also considers mechanisms through which specialization might influence psychological outcomes in young athletes.

# 16-Week Century Training Guide

## Weeks 1-4: Base Building

Start with 3-4 easy, conversational pace rides a week. Over four weeks build up your longest ride to 40-50 miles. Once a week add a hill workout to build strength. More importantly focus on regular effort than intensity. This avoids injury.

## Weeks 5-8: Endurance Development

Move up to 4-5 rides a week. Over four weeks build your longest ride up to 60-75 miles. Add in a tempo ride (steady hard effort) and a hill repeat session. Start experimenting with fueling on your long rides. Try different gels, bars and drinks to see what works for your stomach.

## Weeks 9-12: Peak Building

Over four weeks take up 4-5 rides a week with one hitting 80-90 miles. Add in interval work to improve power and speed. Try climbing longer hills at race pace. To prepare for the century try to ride similar terrain to your race. Test your full nutrition plan.

## Weeks 13-15: Taper and Mental Preparation

Cut weekly mileage back 30-40% but keep up the intensity. Over four weeks build your longest ride up to 50-60 miles. Use this time to focus on recovery e.g. good sleep, stretching and massage. Look at your pacing plan. Try to keep the first half conservative then push harder in the second half.

## Week 16: Race Week

Keep rides short and easy (20-30 miles) during the final week. Take 2-3 days complete rest before the event. Check your gear, nutrition and route. Pack up your support stuff and do a final check of your bike.

## General Tips

Key points over the build up;

- at least one full rest day per week
- good nutrition and hydration
- listen to your body, take additional recovery days if needed
- gradual increase in mileage (max 10% per week)
- ride similar terrain to your century route

More important than fitness will be pacing, fueling and mental preparation. Start conservatively but push hard in the second half.

# 10 Tips for Succulents for Sunny Windowsills

Let's face it, succulents on a sunny windowsill are pretty much ideal for our little green friends. That doesn't mean once you put them there you can leave them alone. Here's how to keep your sun loving succulents happy.

**1. Choose the Right Varieties**

Not all succulents like the same thing. Jade plants, aloe and echeveria thrive in bright light. For your sunniest spots go with the sun-lovers. Yes, they do exist. If your succulent starts to look pale or bleached it could be it's getting too much direct sun. Could try a sheer curtain over it.

**2. Watch for Sunburn**

Every week or two turn your pots over so they grow evenly up the sides. Otherwise they'll tend to lean towards the light like they want out. This is non-negotiable.

**3. Rotate Regularly**

Sunny windowsills dry out quicker but succulents still want their soil on the dry side. So water every 2-3 weeks at most.

**4. Don't Overwater**

Pick up some succulent or cactus mix. Regular potting mix holds too much moisture and is a death trap for succulents.

**5. Use Well-Draining Soil**

Make sure you have a hole in the bottom of your pot. No excuses. Standing water = death.

**6. Check Your Pot's Drainage**

Windowsills can get hot. Depending on summer temps your plants could get stressed. Good air flow will help.

**7. Be Mindful of Heat**

In growing season (spring/summer) every month feed them with diluted succulent fertilizer. That's all.

**8. Feed Lightly**

Check regularly in sunny spots for mealybugs and spider mites.

**9. Watch for Pests**

Let your succulents grow up the side of the pot where they feel comfortable. Some will stretch up, some won't. That's part of their charm.

**10. Embrace Their Natural Growth**

And there you go, happy windowsill succulents!

# Autoplay Features and Intentional Media Habits

Autoplay fundamentally undermines intentional media consumption. By automatically moving on to the next song, episode or video it reduces friction between ending one piece of content and starting another. Passive consumption therefore becomes the easier option.

Whereas with active choice the user creates a decision point to consider whether they want to move on. With autoplay this cognitive checkpoint is removed. Rather than asking themselves "do I want to watch the next episode", users need consciously to interrupt the automatic move on. This shifts the burden away from them. As with all defaults whatever requires least action is disproportionately adopted irrespective of whether it suits the user.

Autoplay also plays on psychological weaknesses. Through continued consumption content becomes more appealing (mere exposure effect). And there is less activation energy in starting new content automatically so enabling what researchers term "binge drift" (far more than intended).

Autoplay isn't always bad though. For more passive activity e.g. background music or regular commutes it improves convenience. But where we need to think about content e.g. more complex media we risk the default becoming autoplay.

The difference is context. Autoplay of instrumental music is quite different to autoplay of narrative shows where often time slips by. To better balance convenience and autonomy platforms could consider an autoplay toggle depending on content type or periodic re-engagement check.

At minimum autoplay features risk undermining intentional habits of more complex media. To restore intentionality either we could rethink defaults on platforms or users consciously turn off these features. More often than not this will require more effort than should be needed through good technological design.

# Hybrid Learning Reshapes the University Lecture Hall

Across universities around the globe we are seeing fundamental rethinking of the traditional lecture as hybrid models of in-person and remote learning increasingly become the norm. This creates more flexible routes for students.

This process accelerated during the pandemic but continues as institutions see real benefits. Rather than replacing lectures with remote learning they are instead rethinking them as more interactive and supported by digital content, recorded lectures and asynchronous learning available to all students whatever location they are studying from.

"More and more we are seeing a shift in how educators think about the large lecture hall," says Dr. Sarah Chen, educational technology researcher at Cambridge University. "Where once it was more about delivering content now it's about building engagement for those present in person and for those joining remotely."

Many institutions now routinely record their lectures meaning students can revisit content at a time convenient for them. For international students this is particularly helpful in overcoming time zone differences. As a result there has been debate about whether attendance at lectures should remain mandatory for academic success.

But some worry hybrid learning risks diminishing value of the university experience. Some academics feel online it is difficult to replicate spontaneous discussions, face-to-face interaction and building a sense of community on campus. "There is risk we could end up with a two-tier system with more limited educational experience for those studying remotely," says Professor James Mitchell of Oxford University.

Taken together these views suggest most university leaders see value in retaining in-person lectures for their collaborative and social value but using technology to add value to learning. More emphasis is now being placed on smaller seminar sessions and lab work as activities best delivered face-to-face. Recorded lectures and online discussion then form the foundation for this.

As universities seek to recover post-pandemic and face budget pressures they could gain efficiency from hybrid learning without necessarily moving away from more traditional academic settings. And in many ways the future lecture hall will be more technologically rich, more accessible and more flexible than ever before. And as a result attending university will look different.

# The Rise of Newsletter Writers as Trusted Commentators

In an age of waning institutional credibility newsletter writers have emerged as unexpectedly trustworthy providers of commentary. Free from the constraints of clicks and corporate interest they have built trust through accountability and authenticity.

Where often mainstream media struggles to engage with its audience newsletter writers regularly build genuine relationships. They invite their readers into their inbox creating an opportunity for more intimate communication. As a result their readers will quickly pick up any errors they make and hold them to account. This feedback loop strengthens incentives for honesty and accuracy which simply don't exist for many in more traditional media.

This is helped by their economic model. Many of the more successful newsletter writers rely on subscription revenue rather than ads meaning they have no incentive to sensationalize or mislead. Their own interests lie in building trust with readers over the long term rather than boosting engagement in the short term. In that sense they have significant advantage over more ad supported media.

Often they bring specialist knowledge of their own chosen field. As a result they can focus on more substantive analysis rather than trying to ride the short term news cycle. Readers value this and increasingly gravitate toward voices who add context and nuance rather than click bait headlines.

That said there are risks in the newsletter ecosystem. With little editorial oversight one could see poor research or unsupported claims. And because entry barriers are low one could see charlatans mixing in alongside genuine experts.

But overall the trend is clear. More and more readers trust independent newsletter writers precisely because they've moved away from the institutional structures undermining much of traditional journalism. As more mainstream media increasingly focuses on engagement over truth the credibility gap it leaves behind is being filled by these more trustworthy writers. That doesn't represent a flaw in information consumption but rather more thoughtful decisions by readers about who they trust.

# Public Transit Funding in Growing Suburbs: A Literature Review

Increasing suburbanization of metropolitan areas across North America and around the globe has brought significant challenges for developing and maintaining transit infrastructure. With growing suburban population there has been increasing demand for accessible, reliable public transport. However funding mechanisms have not kept pace with this demand.

In many respects public transit in the suburbs sits quite differently to in the city. There tends to be lower population densities, more spread out development and historically commuting patterns more suited to the private car. As a result typically much less investment has been made in transit in the suburbs relative to their growing population.

This in turn creates different challenges in funding transit in the suburbs compared with more traditional urban transit. Often existing revenue streams (eg farebox revenue, local taxes and state grants) are insufficient to cover the costs of providing transit in lower density areas with smaller ridership. In recent years some academic work has looked at more diversified funding options e.g. public private partnerships, developer exactions, congestion pricing and regional financing. More recently concerns of climate change and changing commuting patterns (in particular increased use of remote working) have led to fresh consideration of priorities for investment in transit.

Taken together the academic literature shows quite different views of best practice for funding suburban transit. Some argue through more coordinated regional approach and pooled funding resources could be more fairly allocated across different suburban systems. Others argue it is more appropriate for funding to sit at local level and reflect particular characteristics of each suburban context. At state and federal level there is variation in policy supporting ability to invest in transit in the suburbs. In some jurisdictions support for funding transit in the suburbs is strong, in others more limited.

While more recognition is now being given of the role of transit in sustainable development of suburbs there remains considerable scope to improve understanding of which funding mechanisms might be most appropriate for different typologies of suburban area. This review considers the existing academic literature on funding suburban transit. It examines sources of funding, policy innovations and outcomes. Through synthesis of this existing work the review aims to better understand current challenges in funding transit in growing suburban communities and identify potentially useful approaches to support transit development.

# Starting and Maintaining a Neighborhood Book Club

## Getting Started

Start by finding interested neighbors. Put up flyers, include in emails or conversations. Aim for 6-12 people. That should allow scope for discussion but won't become too unwieldy.

Pick up a regular meeting pattern (biweekly or monthly). Choose regular time and place e.g. someone's house, local coffee shop or library.

## Selecting Books

Members suggest a title then vote on which one to read next. Pick different genres each time so it doesn't get repetitive. Think about length and complexity of books. Most groups find 200-300 page novels work well.

Allow enough time to read before each meeting (usually 4-6 weeks). Start meetings with light refreshments to build up community.

## Structuring Meetings

Use 60-90 minutes for discussion of the book. Start with general reactions then steer discussion of themes, characters and writing style. Try and draw quieter members into the discussion.

To keep discussions engaging each meeting pick a discussion leader. They'll need to draw out discussion and keep it focused. Share this role across members so workload isn't too heavy.

## Keeping Momentum

To broaden members' reading pick a mix of popular fiction, classics and less well-known books. Occasionally invite local authors or librarians to talk.

Early on consider expectations of participation. Some people will struggle to commit to regular meetings. If they regularly miss meetings check up on them.

Occasionally vary up meetings e.g. themed potlucks, go along to local author events or arrange video calls with authors. Build up a reading list on goodreads.

## Sustaining Interest

Celebrate e.g. the anniversary of your book club.

As much as literature people join book clubs for community. Build up genuine friendships between members through time spent together outside discussions.

## Handling Challenges

If there's disagreement about book choices remind members different perspectives will add value to discussions. If you feel your group isn't developing consider asking members what they'd like to read and respond appropriately.

Not much work is needed to set up a book club but you'll build up valuable connections in your neighborhood and shared intellectual development.

## 2. Go for a refractor or dobsonian.

Much easier to use than complicated mounts. Intuitive and forgiving so good for new users. Yeah power sounds cool but it's overrated.

## 3. Don't obsess over magnification.

You'll be blown away by a 6 inch reflector even without buying lots of eyepieces. Big lens = better views. Try to get at least 4 inch if you can.

## 4. Aperture matters most.

A cheap scope on a dodgy stand is a recipe for misery. Spend a bit more on a decent mount and your levels of frustration will drop. Check out astronomy forums and youtube.

## 5. Stability is everything.

Real users will tell you straight up which ones aren't so good. Good eyepieces make all the difference. Don't be tempted by the ones included in your scope.

## 6. Read the reviews.

They'll probably be rubbish. Will you take this scope out in the field? If so go for something you could pick up and go.

## 7. Check the eyepieces included.

Don't want to spend 1 hour putting parts together. Really. Members of forums will often let you have a look through their scope, give you honest advice and may even let you borrow one before you buy.

# The Ethics of AI-Generated Artwork in Children's Books

AI generated artwork in children's books raises important ethical considerations worth exploring.

# Key arguments in support

Key arguments in support include efficiency and accessibility. AI tools could cut down production costs opening up the possibility of illustrated children's books for smaller publishers. They could also allow more independent authors to produce illustrated books without needing to commission a professional illustrator.

# Significant concerns

But there are significant concerns. First one needs to consider the risk of displacing jobs from professional illustrators. Often they will not have given permission for their work to be used to train AI systems. Many are already struggling financially so could lose opportunities in this element of the market which traditionally prized human creativity.

Second there is pedagogic value in children's book illustration. Through illustrations young readers learn about representation of themselves and others, of beauty and of diversity. AI systems trained on existing data could reinforce historical biases about for example race, gender and ability.

Third there is a question of value and authenticity. Traditionally in children's literature the author and young reader are seen as sharing important connections. With AI artwork this connection is lost. The book therefore risks losing cultural value.

# Possible ethical routes forward

Possible ethical routes forward could include transparency of when and where AI has been used in creating the book e.g. clear labeling of any illustrations generated through AI so readers can consider how the book has been made. Publishers could also consider a more hybrid use of AI tools to complement rather than replace human artists. Or consider appropriate compensation where they are using existing professional work to train their systems.

# Conclusion

In its own right use of AI artwork in children's books is unlikely to be unethical but requires careful thought about how it is used. To avoid risk one needs to consider alongside innovation, the value of human artists, child development and meaningful representation. Without these considerations the convenience of using AI could prove too costly.

# Right to Repair Movement Gains Momentum as Consumers Embrace Electronics Refurbishment

As e-waste mounts up in landfills across the globe a growing movement is encouraging consumers to repair and refurbish their devices instead of replacing them. This sits at odds with the throwaway culture dominating much of the tech industry for decades.

At its heart the movement is about the right of consumers to repair their own smartphones, laptops and appliances without needing costly services from the manufacturer. Proponents say it reduces e-waste, saves money and allows devices often in perfect working order to be used for longer. "People shouldn't need to buy a new phone if their screen cracks or battery dies," says one repair advocate.

Over recent years there has been the emergence of independent repair shops across cities around the world offering cheaper alternatives to manufacturer service centers. And companies such as iFixit have built up successful businesses selling repair guides and replacement parts.

There is significant environmental value in this approach. E-waste contains toxic substances including lead and mercury and is a major source of pollution. Through device refurbishment consumers could avoid up to 50 pounds of e-waste per person each year according to environmental studies.

Historically manufacturers have resisted such a move saying unauthorized repair risks compromising safety and security of their devices. But through legislative action the landscape is shifting. New York introduced the digital right to repair act and in the EU manufacturers must provide spare parts for some electronics. Tech giants including Apple have started running limited repair schemes but critics argue this is not going far enough.

At the same time there has been huge growth in the market for refurbished electronics. Certified pre-owned devices deliver significant cost saving over new while still meeting quality standards.

Looking forward analysts expect the repair and refurbish market will continue to grow as environmental concerns mount and consumers increasingly question the role of planned obsolescence.

What started as a grassroots movement is now becoming more mainstream. It is beginning to shift how society thinks about consumption and waste of electronics.

# The Hidden Costs of Rent Stabilization

While rent stabilization schemes seek to prevent tenant displacement they produce important economic trade-offs which ultimately damage the housing market and vulnerable groups.

By discouraging property investment and maintenance rent controls restrict supply. Without ability to charge market rent landlords have less incentive to upgrade existing stock and build new housing. This causes shortages in uncontrolled markets pushing up prices elsewhere. As a result housing becomes less affordable overall. This is evidenced in cities such as New York and San Francisco where in areas with strict rent control higher average rents are seen as competition for limited affordable stock intensifies.

Rent stabilization distorts housing allocation. Stabilized units become a scarce commodity. This creates perverse incentives; long term tenants gain an advantage over new residents (often younger and lower income) making it harder for them to move into stabilized stock. As a result labor mobility is reduced as workers are less likely to move for example in search of a new job if they know they won't be able to find affordable housing. Ironically the policy designed to support the poor ends up benefiting those already in housing.

Where rental income is insufficient to fund building improvements maintenance suffers. Landlords cut back on expenditure risking deterioration of the property and neighborhood. Where costs exceed revenue from stabilized rents some landlords withdraw from the market further reducing housing availability.

In addition benefits of rent stabilization fall very unequally. A small minority of tenants on stabilized housing benefit from artificially low rents causing negative externalities for everyone else. Compared with direct assistance programs this is an inefficient way of supporting low income renters and will distort the wider housing market.

At root price controls seek to fix the symptom not the cause. To improve housing affordability supply must be increased through zoning reform, barriers to construction must be reduced and efficiency of development approval must be improved. In this way the availability of affordable housing is increased without artificially creating scarcity.

Rent stabilization is well meaning but has counterproductive effects. Through supply constraints and distortion of housing allocation it ends up harming those it sets out to support and causes wider economic inefficiency. More effective alternatives would focus on expanding supply and targeted assistance for low income renters.

# Literature Review: Community-Supported Fisheries

As concerns grow of unsustainable practices in industrial fishing, lack of sustainability in the food system and declining resilience in communities, community-supported fisheries (CSF) has increasingly been considered by both practitioners and academics as one possible route to more environmentally aware and equitable production and distribution of seafood.

Drawing on the community-supported agriculture (CSA) model, in CSF consumers take shares or memberships of local fishing operations. In return they receive regular deliveries of catch in return for their financial investment and acceptance of risk. Like its agricultural counterpart, CSF sits on changing consumer awareness of food provenance, sustainability and the value of supporting local economies. Unlike more typical supply chains which obscure links between consumer and producer, through CSF there is greater emphasis of transparency, direct links between consumer and producer and shared responsibility for environmental sustainability.

In practice this model helps address a range of sustainability challenges; reducing carbon footprint of seafood distribution, supporting small scale fishers under pressure of competition from industry, and through consumer engagement encouraging more responsible harvesting. CSF is less well researched than its agricultural equivalent. Although there is considerable literature on CSA looking at for example business models, environmental impact and social outcomes, CSF sits across literature in fisheries management, sustainable food systems and economic development. This reflects its more recent emergence as both a practice and subject of academic research.

Taken together existing studies suggest considerable potential for CSF but also important challenges; for example of catch variability, logistical complexity and developing consumer trust of unfamiliar species and variable supply.

In this review the author draws on existing knowledge of community supported fisheries looking at its structure, claims of environmental sustainability, economic viability and social value. Through consideration of perspectives from fisheries science, food systems and community development the review identifies key themes across the existing literature, gaps in knowledge and opportunities for future research of this developing food system model.

# Personal Statement: Art History

Since childhood I have always been drawn to the stories art tells; not just through its beauty but more importantly through the layers of history, culture and human experience in every piece. Through art history I developed the tools to unpick these stories and to see how creativity has shaped civilizations over time.

My own engagement with art history deepened on a visit to the museum where I saw a painting of the Renaissance which I'd only ever seen reproduced in my textbooks. As I stood before the original I realized there were elements I could only pick up from the canvas itself; the brushwork, subtle shifts of color, deliberate composition. And in that moment I realized art history is more than just academic learning. It's a conversation between past and present; between artist and viewer.

What I most value is art as a mirror of society. In one painting we might see the religious beliefs, political tensions, social values of the time it was made. Through art history I could begin to unpick these and build up my own understanding of human civilization. In particular I wanted to explore how through art marginalized voices might have expressed themselves. And now I think more critically about how in their collections museums and other institutions might begin to tell more inclusive stories.

Along with my academic interest I wanted to explore more practically how art history could be used. Through curation of a museum collection, preserving our cultural heritage or working in arts administration I wanted to help different people engage with and find value in art. In our increasingly interconnected world I think we need cultural literacy. Through art history I could start to get under the skin of other perspectives and traditions.

I'd enjoy the challenge of more rigorous study; researching, looking across different periods and mediums and engaging with debates in the academic literature. I'd want to question my own assumptions and develop critical thinking so I could add value in this area.

In essence my desire to study art history reflects my own belief that through art we get some of the most powerful and enduring expression of what it means to be human.

# How to Ask for a Promotion After a Big Project Ships

## Timing Is Everything

Wait two-four weeks after project launch. Time for the dust to settle and for stakeholders to see the results. Don't ask if your manager is stressed or you're in crisis mode.

## Build Your Case

Record your own contribution with specific metrics e.g.
- cost saved/revenue generated
- team members you developed
- problems you fixed up yourself
- improved timeline/budget

Wherever you can include impact e.g "led implementation" could become "led implementation which improved efficiency by 35%"

## Schedule a Formal Conversation

Don't catch your manager off guard. Send them an email "I'd like to talk about my career development and next steps. Do you have 30 minutes this week?" They'll be able to prepare and it shows you're professional.

## Structure the Discussion

Start by showing real pride in the success of the project and your role in it. Then move on to wanting promotion e.g.

"I've enjoyed my role in this project and am proud of what we delivered. I think now I'd be ready for more responsibility so wanted to discuss a move to [specific role]."

## Present Your Value Proposition

To support your case think about:
- track record of good performance
- new skills you've developed
- leadership you've shown
- you've moved on from your original role

## Listen and Respond

Your manager could respond yes, no or "let's think about timing." If they don't immediately say yes ask "what would I need to do to be considered for this promotion." Be specific and ask for clear next steps.

## Follow Up in Writing

Send them an email to recap your discussion and any agreed next steps. This builds accountability and evidence.

## Handle Rejection Gracefully

If they turn you down ask when you could revisit this. Ask for clear criteria against which you could apply in future and agree to work on it.

Remember promotions are for proven performance. Most of your strongest evidence will be from your project. Use it well.

# 10 Tips for Improving Home Audio on a Budget

So you'd like your living room to sound more like a concert hall but your bank account disagrees? Don't worry, good audio doesn't have to cost the earth. Here are some cost effective ways of upping your sound.

## 1. Start with placement.

Before you spend money try moving your speakers. Bass can be boosted in corners and against walls, the most balanced sound is often down the center of the room.

## 2. Add soft furnishings.

Not only do curtains, blankets and rugs make the room more comfortable they also cut down sound reflections and echoes.

## 3. Go wireless.

Think of it as free upgrade. Bluetooth speakers are now very good value and won't cost you as much as more upmarket wired systems.

## 4. Upgrade your source.

Sometimes it's not your speakers that's letting you down but the source. A good lossless audio service or good quality streaming makes a big difference.

## 5. Invest in a budget amplifier.

A small amp can breathe new life into old speakers and now costs little. Good places to pick up bargain vintage speakers are local thrift stores and on facebook marketplace. They'll sound amazing for a fraction of their original price.

## 6. Hunt for used gems.

Make simple fabric wrapped panels using rockwool. Much cheaper than buying ones off the shelf.

## 7. DIY acoustic panels.

Dust affects sound quality so with a bit of regular maintenance you'll improve it.

## 8. Clean your equipment.

Good quality doesn't always mean expensive but avoid the cheapest stuff as it can cause interference.

## 9. Check your cables.

Don't forget this... often a bit of soft material and furniture placement will trump expensive kit.

## 10. Room treatment matters most.

And more often than not smart spending beats big spending. Start small, listen and strategically upgrade. Your ears (and bank account) will thank you.

# Inbox Overload: A Modern Workplace Problem

Inbox overload is now a common complaint across the workplace. It arises from a range of factors in our increasingly digital age. First, the low barrier to sending an email and its accessibility means anyone can send messages to anyone else. Often they do so without much thought. As a result we see increasing numbers of messages sent where perhaps just one more detailed daily briefing would have sufficed. Copying multiple people and sending non urgent messages has become common.

This is worsened by the always on culture driven by smartphones and notifications. Employees feel they need to check their email constantly risking blurring the boundary between work and home. Messages which previously would have formed part of one daily briefing now filter through through the day and into the evening. This fragments attention.

Often companies themselves fail to set up clear guidelines on when different communication channels should be used. As a result people default to email for everything from simple questions to more complex discussions which would be better handled through meetings or via instant messaging. This leads to unnecessary repetition and noise.

And increasingly we see automated emails flood in. System alerts, newsletters, promotional material and automated alerts increasingly clog up inboxes making it harder to pick up important messages.

Without a culture of effective email management many workers lack strategies for dealing with large volumes of emails. Features such as "reply all" and sending group emails can lead to endless chain of replies. And the expectation we should respond quickly to email creates anxiety. Workers worry they need to keep their inbox at zero or will miss something important. They therefore increasingly treat email as an urgent form of communication rather than asynchronous.

# Charging Into the Future: How Older Neighborhoods Are Adapting to Electric Vehicles

With increasing uptake of electric vehicles across the country we're seeing some unique challenges in older residential neighborhoods to keep pace with the shift to green energy.

Many established urban and suburban communities lack the parking space and electrical capacity to support widespread charging. Residents often rely on street parking and have older electrical grids not designed to cope with increased demand.

"Homeowners without driveways will struggle to fit private chargers and many cities haven't yet rolled out enough public chargers," says Maria Chen, director of urban planning at the Clean Energy Institute.

Already some municipalities are acting. Over the next two years Portland, Oregon will roll out 50 public charging stations in disadvantaged neighborhoods. And building owners in New York City are being encouraged to retrofit older apartment complexes to include charging.

Community groups are also getting involved. The Boston EV Access Initiative works with local groups to look at best locations for charging infrastructure and calls for more even access across income groups.

But there are challenges. Retrofitting old electrical systems is costly. Installing a charger can cost more than $2,000. And some residents worry about aesthetics and safety of charging infrastructure at street level.

Undeterred advocates say these neighborhoods are some of the most diverse and walkable in our cities. They believe investment in their charging infrastructure is both environmentally necessary and socially fair.

As more people move to electric vehicles it will be important we support all neighborhoods through this transition if we are to meet our climate ambitions and avoid leaving any community behind in the clean energy revolution.
